Afghanistan—Minister of Foreign Affairs

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Honourable members, I have much pleasure in informing the House
that His Excellency Dr Zalmai Rassoul, Mini ster of Foreign Affairs from the Afghan
National Assembly, is within the precincts of this Chamber. I am sure members would
wish him to be welcomed and accorded a seat on the left of the Chair.
His Excellency Dr Zalmai Rassoul, accompanied by Assistant Speaker Tisch, entered
the Chamber and took a seat on the left of the Chair.
Economy—IMF 2013 Preliminary Concluding Statement
1. MAGGIE BARRY (National—North Shore)  to the Minister of Finance: What
reports has he received on the economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Today the International
Monetary Fund released its preliminary concluding statement on New Zealand. The
report concludes that New Z ealand’s fiscal reduction path  strikes the right balance
between limiting debt increases while sustaining economic growth. The report says:
“We regard the planned pace of … defici t reduction as striking the right balance
between sustaining output growth and limiting public debt growth, and consistent with a
framework where monetary policy plays a pr imary role in managing aggregate demand.
The benefits of the plan are many.”

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What does the IMF say are the bene fits of the planned reduction in
the Budget deficit?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The IMF cites four benefits: firstly, it withdraws fiscal
stimulus at the right time by making room fo r the expected increases in private sector
and earthquake-related construction spendi ng; secondly, it reduces pressure on
monetary policy—

items.speaker: Andrew Williams
items.text: Who wrote this?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: —thirdly, it creates fiscal space to manage increasing age
and health-related costs and to  cope with negative shocks; and, fourthly, it helps raise
national savings and reduce the current account  deficit. And in answer to the member
over there, it was written by the IMF.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What are the key risks the IMF identifies for the New Zealand
economy, and what are the options for managing those risks?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The IMF identifies two main near-term risks to the New
Zealand economy. These are potential weakne sses or a worsening in the financial
conditions in the world economy. The IMF al so identifies risk in the New Zealand
housing market, noting that supply bottlenecks persist and prices remain elevated. The
IMF notes that New Zealand has room to resp ond to shocks with its monetary policy,
and the level of public debt leaves room for fiscal polic y response. The floating New
Zealand dollar is also seen as an effective buffer. The IMF also says that our
fundamentals have improved si nce the global financial cris is. Household and business
8602 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Mar 2013
balance sheets have strengthened, and banks  have reduced their foreign funding and
been assisted by a strong growth in deposits and slower growth in credit.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: What does the IMF say about the value of the New Zealand dollar?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The IMF shares the Government’s view that the dollar is at
a high value, largely because of factors outside our control. In particular, the strength of
the New Zealand dollar is determined by the relative weaknesses of other currencies and
other economies, many of which are printi ng money. As it says, if global monetary
policy were to become less stimulatory, the exchange rate would likely depreciate over
time. The IMF also notes that the Government ’s return to surplus is easing pressure on
the exchange rate by boosting national savings.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Does he agree with the IMF that “… New Zealand has run
persistent current account deficits resulting in  net external liabilities which are high by
international standards. The deficit is expected to widen this year despite relatively
strong terms of trade …”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, and I would note that those were largely due to the
previous Government when the balance of pa yments deficit rolled out to over 8 percent
of GDP. I really think the member should st op this line of questioning because all he
does is point out that the Opposition are lousy economic managers.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. The Minister was
asked about the future proj ections, so, surely, he cannot go back to a former
Government from 4 years ago and think he can get away with it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! He referred to the IMF report, which talked about persistent
current account deficits over many years. I think the question was adequately addressed.
Education System—Accountability
2. BRENDAN HORAN (Independent)  to the Minister of Education : Is
accountability within our education system paramount?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Accountability is paramount
in so far as everyone in the education system  needs to be accountable for achieving the
best results for all New Zealand children. For example, nationa l standards provide
parents with information as to how their children are doing, which helps provide
accountability. I am sure the member woul d support the general concept of parents
knowing exactly what their children are up to.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Will the Minister show her acc ountability by revealing to this
House the expensive reasons why staff around her are being paid to leave?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: The member will be aware th at staffing matters regarding
ministerial offices are the responsibility of the Department of Internal Affairs.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: What steps is the Government taking to strengthen accountability
for raising achievement?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Our Government is doing a number of things to ensure every
child in New Zealand gets a great education. We have set Better Public Services targets
at early childhood education, National Certif icate of Educational Achievement level 2,
and New Zealand Qualifications Framework level 4. We are putting more money into
education than ever before, and we are clearer about what we want as a result of it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Is a sound education and understanding of accountability
for other people’s money and assets paramount within our education system, and why is
that important?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: Yes. It is important because we  are all elected by the people of
New Zealand and we need to ensure we are accountable as members of Parliament.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: If we are all accountable to the people of New Zealand for the
decisions we make, will the Minister of  Education resign her position given the
19 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8603
taxpayer now has to fork out $11 million to fix up the mess she has made with
Novopay?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: No. When we look at the issue of Novopay, we have done a
huge amount. The Minister responsible fo r Novopay, Steven Joyce, today announced a
superb package of support for schools, and we are very proud of that package.

items.speaker: Brendan Horan
items.text: Will the Minister show accountability and assure the House that, as
Ombudsman David McGee stated, it is unaccepta ble for there to be any suggestion that
a Government department must bypass the Official Information Act, and can she
guarantee that that will not happen with education in this term?

items.speaker: Hon NIKKI KAYE
items.text: The member will be aware that these matters are before the
Education and Science Committee,  and I think that of all the members in this House
who care about due process, it would be that one.
Prime Minister—Statements on Solid Energy and Novopay
3. DAVID SHEARER (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by all his statements?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I do stand by all my statements, and in
that I include bank statements.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I want to hear the question.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that one of the three problems with
Solid Energy was that it “added gearing to  a company that historically had not had
gearing”, or is Tony Ryall right when he sa id that debt was not the cause of Solid
Energy’s problems?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Both are correct. In the case of Solid Energy, debt did not
cause the collapse of the company, but if there was not debt, the Government would not
have to be in the restructuring process that we are in.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Did his Minister of Finance appr ove the sending of a letter to Solid
Energy indicating his expectati on that it would “increase their gearing from current
levels,”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My understanding is that Si mon Power as the Associate
Minister of Finance actually sent it, not the Minister of Finance—yes. That looks pretty
consistent, from what I can see, with the lette r that Mr Mallard sent where he said that
the indications were that the gearing shoul d be around about 35 percent, and, in fact,
that the dividends should be around about 65 percent of profits.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: When the Prime Minister said it was unfortunate that Mr Shearer
forgot to disclose—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] Order!

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not believe I need assistance. The Prime Minister certainly has
no responsibility for that matter.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: Supplementary question, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Does the ACT Party have
two supplementary questions today?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, I have ruled that one out.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: No, no. You have ru led it out. You let him ask it and you
ruled it out. At that point, it is gone. You did not invite him to rephrase it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The ACT Party has one question. The member can seek leave if he
so wishes. [Interruption] Order! There is one supplementa ry question. It has been used
up. It was ruled out of order. If the memb er wishes to have another supplementary
question, he will have to seek leave to do so.
8604 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Mar 2013

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: I seek leave to do so. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Although it was pretty
clear from the few words that the Hon John Banks got out—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I have ruled.

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I realise you have ruled. I just  want to get a clarification
about where we are going from here. Although it was clear that Mr Banks was going to
raise a matter that has been of interest in the news recently—and you were quick to then
suggest and, in fact, rule it out, assuming that there was no link to anything the Prime
Minister had said. On other occasions, notab ly over the last few weeks, you have given
Opposition members an opportunity to rephras e their questions up to three times. I
wonder whether it would be possible for Mr Banks to get similar treatment.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I thank the member for his assistance. On this occasion I have ruled;
we will move on. The questioner, an experienced member, raised a question that clearly
was not going to be in order, so he has lo st that opportunity. He has sought leave. The
House has the opportunity to so decide, and has done so.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. This is not to
challenge your ruling, because I want to disc uss the fact that Mr Banks sought leave. If
he had gone on to explain that he wanted to talk about the Kim Dotcom affair—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That is not a point of order.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Can he confirm that the financial performance measures for State-
owned enterprises, including Solid Energy, announced in June 2010 explicitly tell
boards that they would be judged according to their gearing rati o and that the Crown
expected a gearing ratio of around 40 percent?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: From memory that reflects—though I do not have the letter—
the letter that was sent. I think it is also wo rth recalling that Mr Palmer, the chairman of
Solid Energy, actually wrote back to Mr Po wer and made it quite clear that gearing
ratios and matters of the balance sheet were the sole preserve of the company and not
the Government.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he agree with the Dece mber 2008 Treasury report that the
appointments to State-owned enterprise board s are the single most important lever that
Ministers have for influencing State-owned enterprise performance?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am not sure I would say it is the single most important lever.
I think it is a very important lever, and that  is one of the ones that this Government has
followed by making, I think, pretty sound appoi ntments where possible. But there are
other levers, of course, that the Government can pull.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: If his Government is so dissatisfied with the board’s approach, as he
is suggesting, why did it reappoint five of the member s after 2008 and reappoint the
chair, John Palmer, not once but twice?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The member is giving different  time-scales on what has taken
place—[Interruption] Well, he gets confused with numbers—I will tell you that for
nothing. But anyway—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There are different time-scale s, but what is quite clear—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Would you allow the Prime Minister to please answer the
question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What is clear is that during a period of time the company—in
this case, Solid Energy—had aspirations to change the fabric of that company into
something far greater and far more audacious than was the case of the Government. In
the case of the Government, we pushed back on those issues. That did not mean that we
did not have faith in the board, but what it did say was that we did not agree with the
19 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8605
plan it was under. When we ultimately went through the mixed-ownership model and
had the scoping study, it was at that point that  we absolutely determined that there were
bigger issues in terms of that company if we were going to go through the mixed-
ownership model with that company.

items.speaker: David Shearer
items.text: Does he seriously expect New Zealanders to believe that the
Government demands that the company incr ease its debts, prom ises to judge the
company on that debt, and then, when the company’s debt increases by $178 million in
a single year, says that these are all somehow unrelated events?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: What is true with Solid Energy is that the board and
management have sole responsibility for the quality of decision making that they do in
terms of investments. What is also true is that we did not demand an increase in gearing;
we followed exactly the same process th at Trevor Mallard did, which was the
recommendations from Treasury, and the compa ny made it clear that it would make its
own decisions. In the end, if the member is wanting—[ Interruption] Well, the member
has been running around the count ry saying that the problem is  that we want dividends,
when for months beforehand he was saying that the great thing about State-owned
enterprises is they pay dividends. I mean, you cannot have it both ways, Mr Shearer.
You cannot have an account in New York and an account—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. You earlier ruled out one
area of questioning. The Prime Mi nister started off out of order, you brought him back
into line, and he finished up out of order. I wonder whether, Mr Speaker, this is an
indication of new standards; if so—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The last part of the Prim e Minister’s answer was certainly
not helpful to the order of the House. Further supplementary questions?

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Supplementary—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! Supplementary question, Metiria
Turei.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Tēnā koutou e te Whare. Given the Prime
Minister said yesterday that today was not D-Day for Novopay, when can New
Zealanders expect a decision on Novopay such  that they will ha ve confidence that
schools will no longer be burdened with this failed system?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Can the member please give the date when I actually said that
statement? I do not recall saying it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, in the question she said it was yesterday, as I understood.
Does the member want to repeat the question for the benefit of the Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It is not a question of
repeating it. I do not believe I ever said it. If the member can tell me when I said it I will
respond to it.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is a satisfactory answer.

items.speaker: Hon John Banks
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. You have just asked whether
the member wants to rephrase the question—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, I thought the Prime Minister n eeded it rephrased. He has said
he disagrees with the question. We are moving on. He has satisfactorily answered it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: When can principals, teachers, and families expect from his
Government either a thumbs up or a thumbs down on Novopay? It is not too much to
ask for some certainty for families.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We are working our way through those issues. As the Minister
announced today, the Government is coming to the party with a significant cash
offering to schools to try to help them through the process.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: What a botch-up.
8606 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Mar 2013

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Well, that was the botch-up that you guys started, actually; we
will just tidy it up. But you do not want to hear about that, do you, “Chippy”?
Anyway—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. The Prime Minister did not
address my question, which was when—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Prime Minister very adequately addressed the question.
Climate Change—Drought Conditions and Government Response
4. Dr RUSSEL NORMAN (Co-Leader—Green) to the Minister of Finance: Does
he stand by his response that human-induced climate change “may well be” real?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, the Minister stands by
his full statement, in which he also said: “The  fact is that the Government is assisting
farmers with short-term emergency-type assistance through a dr ought. If there is a
succession of droughts farmers would need to change their farming practice;
Government assistance will not protect them from the consequences of it.”

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Why cannot he simply say yes, that he accepts the basic fact
that human-induced climate change is happen ing, and that it is causing more frequent
and more intense droughts?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think the second part of that member’s question is open to
debate, actually, by a whole ra nge of experts. The point th at the Minister was making
last week in response to the member’s previous question is that in terms of the current
drought the contribution by climate change is  not as material as dealing with the
drought. I think that is a very fair response.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, then, in relation to his answer to that question, does he
disagree with the National Institute of Wate r and Atmospheric Research when it states:
“Droughts are projected to become more frequent and more intense under climate
change.”?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No. The point that he was making is that the climate has
many changes: firstly, year-t o-year variability, and longer- term climate change. These
are things that farmers have dealt with si nce time immemorial. Also, farmers deal with
other things including economic change and technology change. They no longer, for
example, use horses to pull ploughs, which ma y come as news to the member. But the
reality is all these things change, and farmers are capable of coping with those changes.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Does he think that 97.4 percen t of climate scientists in an
international survey who think that human-induced climate change is real were being far
too definite and maybe they should have said it just “may well be” happening?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure which rabbit hole the member is trying to
chase the Minister down at this point. There is no issue in terms of the work that is
being done by climate scientists around the world. The only questions are, firstly,
whether this particular drought is caused by climate-change, and, secondly, whether the
actual cause of it is as relevant at this point as the mitigation measures that are taken to
help farmers through it. I think the Minister made the point that it was the mitigation
measures that he was focused on.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, does he understand—to he lp the Minister—that the
particular hole that I am trying to chase th is rabbit down is the hole that says climate
change causes more droughts and more intens e droughts, so the drought that we have
just seen is more likely to occur in the fu ture, so the Government needs an adaptation
plan? Does he have an adaptation plan?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: The reality is that I do not think anybody yet knows
whether this drought is a c onsequence of anthropogenic cl imate change or not. The
19 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8607
reality is that there is a dr ought this year. If there were  a succession of droughts, then
obviously there would be further need to adjust. The Government has a number of
adjustment measures, including  a huge amount of work go ing on in the water-quality
space with the farming community—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Irrigation.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: There are irrigation proposals that are being advanced as
we speak, and, more generally, there are also  adaptation proposals. The Minister makes
the other point that, actual ly, people—individuals and businesses—are very good at
doing adaptation as well.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: Well, then, was US President Obama right when he said in
relation to this issue: “We can choose to believe that Superstorm Sandy, and the most
severe drought in decades, and the worst wildfires some states  have ever seen were all
just a freak coincidence. Or  we can choose to believe in  the overwhelming judgment of
science—and act before it’s too late.”? When will he act?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not qualified to comment  on the President’s view of
the Sandy storm, but what I w ould point out is that, actua lly, in terms of individual
weather events, whether it is a drought or whether it is a flood, I would very much doubt
that many scientists would link those to climate change. What they would link it to is
climate change over a period, and there is no argument with that. Again, I cannot think
why the member is wasting all his supplementary questions on it.
Canterbury Hospitals—Redevelopment
5. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: What progress can he re port on the Christchurch Hospital redevelopment
project?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The first site work on Christchurch’s
$600 million - plus hospitals redevelopment proj ect will start before the middle of this
year. Cabinet has agreed to set aside around $500 million for the largest and most
complex building project in the history of the New Zealand public health service. The
rebuild will certainly go a long way to setti ng Canterbury health se rvices back on their
feet after the 2010 and 2011 earthquakes.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What will the Christchurch redevelopment project involve?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The work will include 159 new beds for Burwood and
Christchurch Hospitals and eight extra operating theatres. Construction of a new facility
for older people’s health is being fast track ed at Burwood Hospital, with site clearing
beginning mid-year and completion in 2015. Ch ristchurch Hospital’s development, or
redevelopment, includes a new, expanded intensive care unit and emergency
department, purpose-designed space for paedia trics, eight new operating theatres, in-
patient wards, and new outpatient facilities; and is due for completion in 2018.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Will the rebuild of Ashburton Hospital be funded from the $600
million announced yesterday; if not, what fu nding, if any, has been allocated by the
Government for Ashburton Hospital?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Ashburton Hospital will be rebuil t. It is my expectation that
the funding will be a combination of district  health board and Ministry of Health
funding, as that member has known. She has put out a statement saying the services
were not going to be rebuilt—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. That was a pretty straight
question, I think you will find, and there was no need for the political cant that
followed.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is true, and it was adequate ly answered. The last part was not
necessary.
8608 Questions for Oral Answer 19 Mar 2013
KiwiRail—Health and Safety
6. DARIEN FENTON (Labour)  to the Minister of Transport : Does he have
confidence in KiwiRail’s health and safety standards; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes, but there is always
room for improvement.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Has he seen reports that 10 workers could have died of carbon
monoxide poisoning during work fo r KiwiRail on the Kaimai t unnel last year; if so, is
he satisfied that KiwiRail followed proper safety procedure in this case?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: I have seen a report on th e incident that occurred in
the Kaimai tunnel. I have seen a press re lease from the Labour Party suggesting that
death could have occurred. I think the press release is somewhat alarmist. The people
who were in that situation ha d been given instruction in gas awareness for tunnel work,
and adequate safety equipment was issued to all persons who were in the tunnel at that
time.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Is he aware that KiwiRail’s ow n investigation found some of the
group were not trained in tunne l gas awareness, as they were supposed to be, and there
was no KiwiRail staff member in charge to is sue safety gear and train the workers, as
per KiwiRail’s own instructions?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: What I am aware of is that the person in charge of the
contracted group had just completed tunnel gas awareness training and been certified as
competent. The second group of concrete  resin injection specialists, although not
specifically trained in tunnel awareness, were under the direct supervision of the trained
contractor and they did comply with the rule s. At the time of the incident they were
trained, as was the requirement at the time. KiwiRail has conducted significant
investigations into this, and all of the recommendations from those considerations are
being implemented.

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Is he aware that the workers were exposed to high levels of gas
because they exited the tunnel in the wrong direction, and that KiwiRail’s own
investigation found this was because the evacuation plan was not created appropriately?

Roading—Newmarket Viaduct and Christchurch Southern Motorway
7. PAUL GOLDSMITH (National)  to the Minister of Transport : What progress
has the Government made on improving roading infrastructure?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Last Friday the Prime
Minister opened the Newmarket Viaduct.  The $244 million Newmarket project marks
the southern end of the centr al motorway junction, the busie st section of motorway in
New Zealand. At its northern end is the Victoria Park Tunnel, which was opened in late
2011. The Government’s roads of national si gnificance programme is progressing, and
these two roads were part of that progr amme. In between both are a host of other
19 Mar 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 8609
motorway improvements, and combined they provide much better transport connections
around and through Auckland, improving traffi c flows between State Highway 1 and
State Highway 16, and ensuring freight can move  a lot more efficiently in and out of
Auckland’s container port. Removing the ol d viaduct at Newmarket and constructing
the new one, with only a minimum of disrupti on to traffic on the southern motorway, is
a remarkable achievement in engineering and innovation. It al so has very good
environmental outcomes.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: What benefits can motorists exp ect from improvements to roading
infrastructure?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Although it will take some time to measure
completely the improvements that Newmar ket’s viaduct will provide, significant time
savings are being reported, thanks to the Government’s opening of the motorways for
Victoria Park and indeed in Christchurch, as well. Also, there is about 3.5 minutes being
saved on the Te Rapa bypass, and motorists are experiencing that time saving also in the
cost of fuel. This is a focus that we think is very, very good for the economy. It certainly
makes travelling on our roads much safer also.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Did any other roading improve ments report a time saving to
motorists?

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Yes. Earlier this year, I opened stage one of the
Christchurch Southern Motorway, another on e of the Government’s roads of national
significance, and already truck drivers are reporting time savings of up to 15 minutes
between Rolleston and the Port of Lyttelton. This would represent a saving of nearly 10
litres of fuel. The Government is committed to  improving our infrastructure and this is
demonstrated in the savings and benefits to New Zealanders, which are quite obvious.

11. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : How is
the Government’s Social Workers in Hosp itals initiative making a difference for
vulnerable children?

items.text: The social workers
in hospitals initiative was introduced by National in 2009. We now have a Child, Youth
and Family social worker based in every di strict health board in the country. When
hospitals admit children, if staff have care and protection concerns , the social worker
engages with the family and hospital st aff. In the last 6 months of 2012, 7,386
consultations took place about families th ey were worried about. As a result, 1,059
reports of concern were made to Child, Youth and Family.

items.text: What feedback has she received about  front-line staff working together
to better protect vulnerable children?

items.text: Feedback from health profes sionals shows that there is a

social workers are a welcome part of the team. Last week I visited Palmerston North
Hospital and met with one of our social work ers and with health professionals there.

fact that they can get in earlier when that concern is there, make a difference, and get
the right support in place so that that, in many cases, very young baby is safe when they
go home.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Chairperson. One of the major changes
that the Ministry for the Environment is wo rking on as part of its policy under this
Government is to change the way in which planning is done under the Resource
Management Act so that Mi nisters would have much mo re power to intervene and
direct councils to amend or change their plans. Instead of the ministry developing policy
statements and national environmental standards so that we have consistent
environmental policy around New Zealand, we w ould have the Minist er being able to
intervene to pick an d choose winners—to potentially di rect the Northland councils to
promote mining in their plans, or Hawke’s Bay to have policies that would make it
easier for mega, think-big, risky schemes like Ruataniwha to proceed, or in Auckland
for the Minister to be able to smash the metropolitan urban limits in order to allow
urban sprawl, when the council had specifically put those lim its in place to avoid urban
sprawl. As prominent Bluegreens member a nd former ministerial adviser Guy Salmon
has said: “This is what they do in China.”
This is worse than the National Developmen t Act in the Muldoon era. And it is this
ministry, under this Government, that is promoting these substantive changes to the
Resource Management Act, and also prop osing to strip out five of the key
environmental principles in the heart of th e Act—the purpose section in Part 2. These
changes are deeply troubling be cause they potentially promot e the politicisation of the
Public Service and the minist ry, and the potential for more dodgy backroom deals, as
we have seen with Skycity. When you have a ministry that has got only 280-odd staff,
and those staff are based in Wellington—the ministry does not have any regional offices
in Christchurch or in Auckland any more—it is  simply not credible to believe that the
ministry would be adding value on the spec ific challenges that we have on land
8618 Financial Review Debate 19 Mar 2013
management, water management, and coastal management in a particular region by
giving these powers to the Minister. The powers will not be promoting—
Report noted.
Ministry for Primary Industries
Hon DAMIEN O’CONNOR (Labour—West Coast - Tasman) : A little over 2
weeks ago we had a very revealing document ta bled in this House that says more about
the Government’s management of primary i ndustries than anything else. It came from
the Auditor-General, which is probably the organisation with the most credibility across
this nation, and that document was very revealing. Of course, it stated the obvious—that
our country is more dependent on biosecur ity than any other developed country. It
stated: “it is my view that MPI is under-p repared for potential incursions from some
high-risk organisms.” The response of the Minister in the chair, the Minister for Primary
Industries, was that since the year 2000, f unding for biosecurity has doubled. And do
you know what? That is the trut h. What he failed to say wa s that all of that funding
occurred under a Labour Government and that the first thing that the National
Government did on coming in was to slas h $2 million from front-line biosecurity
services.
I will quote part 3 of the document: “The Ministry has lacked a strategic approach to
capability. This includes workforce planning and, with some exceptions, its approach to
information and information technology. Both of  these areas represent serious risks for
the Ministry.” Well, they are greater risks for the country, particularly when you go over
the page, where you read, again: “The lack of  realistic business planning also affected
the preparation of new response plans … Insufficient resources have meant that many of
the plans have not been comple ted or tested to ensure that they are fit for purpose.”
Each and every day we are under huge threat from biosecurity incursions that could
cripple this economy.
Yesterday the Minister’s department fought  the pork industry to allow pork imports
from countries that have PRRS—porcine  reproductive and respiratory syndrome—a
disease that costs the US industry $600 million every year. The ministry fought the pork
industry to lower the import health standard s to allow pork that might satisfy a few
supermarkets and a few pork industry trader s. It is simply not good enough that the
National Government slashes funding for biosecurity and allows and oversees a
ministry that is ill-prepared for these. It st ates in the report that we are ill-prepared for
an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, let alone the increa sed risk from things like
porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome.
It is a shocking indictment on a Nationa l Government that claims to be the
representative party of the primary producers that it has stood by and ignored the
realities of this report, which we have know n about for some time. It has been slashing
funding for biosecurity, and for the Minister  to get up and say that funding has doubled
since 2000 but fail to say th at almost every one of t hose dollars occurred under a
Labour-led Government—not National—is an insult to the good people who run
biosecurity services up and down this count ry. They know full well the risks that we
incur from visitors, from imports, and from everyday trade, let alone the determination
by the Ministry for Primary Industries to allow in pork under reduced import health
standards and to allow Australian honey with the diseases that might come from that.
We have facing us every day an example of the failure of a ministry that gave us
reassurance time and time again that it wa s world class through Psa. We have a
kiwifruit industry that has been devastated by Psa and by a Government department that
failed and was incapable of assessing the ri sks. The Auditor-Gener al has said quite
clearly that unless something is  done to increase the resources —it is stated here in the
19 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8619
report—there are insufficient resources to  carry out the planning necessary. The
Government must put more funding into biosecurity. It must raise the bar because of the
increased levels of visitation by people from  countries like China or you name it. We
have, every day, coming into this country pa lm kernel expeller, or PKE, which is
needed for cows. That is understandable, as we have droughts and we have shortages of
feed. But the ministry is in no way prepared  to assess and prepare for the risks that
might come through foot-and-mouth disease.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: It is an opportunity for
me to respond to the member Damien O’ Connor, who has just resumed his seat,
because I think that Mr O’Connor wants to pl ay politics with what is a very serious
issue. Actually, I cha llenge Mr O’Connor as to whether he has actually read the whole
report or just read the executive summary. If Mr O’Connor has read the whole report, he
will realise that the Auditor-General actually said that we have got a pretty good system,
and there are seven recommendations that I and the Director-General of the Ministry for
Primary Industries have said we will ta ke on board. What Mr O’Connor fails to
recognise—what he fails to recognise—is th at we do have a worl d-class biosecurity
system.
Hon Damien O’Connor: No, we don’t.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Yes, we do. The Auditor-General was sitting in the room
when we ran the foot-and-mouth exercise ca lled Exercise Taurus last year, and as a
result of that exercise we are adopting a lot of the learnings from that, unlike when that
member was last in Government. When that member was last in Government, it is
worthwhile noting that it ran a simulation on foot-and-mouth. What was interesting was
that those recommendations just sat on th e shelf. The 2005 recommendations under
Labour from running a foot-and-mouth disease exercise were not even adopted. They
were not even adopted. How dare that member come down into this Chamber and say
that we are sitting on our hands? Becaus e that is not true. We will take these
recommendations. We will take them seriously. I say to the member that this is my No.
1 priority—biosecurity. How dare that member  come in here and say that we are not
prepared?
I want to raise another issue with him, a nd that is about capability. Last year the
Ministry for Primary Industries employed an  extra 45 new quarantine inspectors, 11
more were recruited in January this year, se ven detector dog handler s were recruited as
well, and there are a further four—11 new de tector dogs have gra duated as well. We
take our biosecurity and our border control extremely seriously.
Importantly, what I want to say is that ri ght now the country is under a pretty severe
state of drought, and it is good that it has rained. It is fantastic. What it will do, this
rainfall, is a couple of things. One, it wi ll lift the spirits of rural communities. The
second thing is that we will get pasture grow ing as well, which is hugely important. We
do not have a shortage of rainfall in this coun try. We have a storage issue. We need to
store rain in the winter months and utilis e it in the summer months. It is good for our
economic growth. It is good for our environment. It is pretty simple. But when you look
at Labour, I am pretty sure it is opposed. Here is a question for Damien O’Connor.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, no.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: Does Damien O’Connor support irrigation schemes or not?
Hon Damien O’Connor: You answer the questions, Minister.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: He cannot answer it. Damien O’Connor is silent because here
is what his finance spokesman, David Parker, sa id recently: “its ill-considered subsidies
that are coming from the taxpayer dollar to ir rigation schemes,”. That is what Labour
thinks. So right now the country is pretty much under a drought—although let us hope it
is breaking—and Labour is not prepared to help rural, regional communities invest in
8620 Financial Review Debate 19 Mar 2013
irrigation schemes, unlike this Government. We have said: “Here is $80 million to kick-
start some of these regional irrigation sche mes.” We would like to see that go to $400
million. We believe we can increase the pr oductivity and look after the environment
better with these regional irrigation schemes. There are about 400,000 hectares where
we can lift our productivity and improve the wa ter quality of our freshwater rivers, yet
Labour is not prepared to back rural New Zealand—shameful.
What we are also debating right now out in our communities is a generational change
in water and fresh water, and also the Res ource Management Act as well. This is the
once-in-a-generation water reform that we are having pretty good dialogue about across
New Zealand at the moment. I wish to acknowledge the Land and Water Forum, which
has worked hard on this issue over the last 4 years. It has done fantastic work and we
need to acknowledge that. The biggest issue that we are talking about up and down New
Zealand in terms of fresh water and storag e is to do with water quality and water
quantity. We are getting very, very good feedback.
Overall, water is just one part of grow ing our economic development. We have a
very ambitious target of increasing our exports from 30 percent to 40 percent of GDP by
2025. The primary industry, of course, we all know plays a huge part—72 percent of
merchandise exports. We are a nation of around 4.5 million people, and we feed about
40 million people around the world. We export to 160 markets. We are recognised here
in New Zealand as a bit of a world leader  in innovation and food safety standards.
Indeed, recently I have just been over to Latin America wi th the Prime Minister and a
business delegation of about 25. It becomes very  apparent that we are world leading in
our food safety standards. We carefully manage the impacts of our production on the
environment. We have a real emphasis on an imal welfare as well and looking after our
animals. And we have a world-class biosecurity system.
If you think about where we have come from since the 1980s, when we had those big
reforms—and that is what happens when we get on the world stage; they want to learn
from us what happened in the 1980s and how we adjusted—the important point is that
now we are exporting the same amount of la mb meat as we did in the 1980s, but from
about half the number of sheep. When you ge t on the world stage, they look down on
little old New Zealand and think that we  are fantastic with  our innovation, our
technology, and lifting our producti vity. That is why this G overnment has invested in
the Primary Growth Partnership. That is th e Government investing side by side with
industry. It has been hugely  successful. There are 13 pr ojects up and running as we
speak, and $650 million invested in collab oration with the Government and the
industry. That has been extremely worthwhile.
We think about the Latin American trip. What became hugely important to me when
I got into places like Colombia, where most of the countries have a huge amount of land
that is undeveloped, is that they  are very keen to foster jo int ventures and partnerships
with New Zealand, because they realise that we have this wealth of experience in
innovation and technology. That is going to be the future. We  already have a very close
working relationship with Chile. Chile is pr etty much a cousin of New Zealand. You
think about Colombia, when President Santos stands up and says they want to see a
free-trade agreement with New Zealand. That is absolutely fantastic because of the huge
potential for New Zealand in Latin America, particularly in Colombia. What we have
also signalled that we are keen to invest in in Colombia is $4 million, with some aid
money, to get this technology and expertise to work with  their farmers closely. The
signal that I have got from Colombia is 150 of  their farmers are keen to come down to
New Zealand. We can showcase all of the good work that we do in our primary
industries.
19 Mar 2013 Financial Review Debate 8621
In conclusion, New Zealand is extremely well placed on the world stage. It was a
very successful trip to Latin America, with some deliverables to come from those 25-
odd business groups that travelled with us. Th ey had something like 138 meetings, and
about 42 now have concrete leads that they can follow up to continue to work on joint
ventures and partnerships with these countries of Latin America.
I am very ambitious for the primary i ndustries. We have got a world-class
biosecurity system, we will adopt the reco mmendations from the Auditor-General, and
we will continue to make  improvements. This Government is backing rural New
Zealand. This Government cares about rural New Zealand. La bour does not care,
because it does not back irrigation projects. The Greens do not care, because they do not
believe that irrigation projects are sust ainable. Rural New Z ealand knows that the
Greens and Labour, coming together with New Z ealand First, will mean a capital gains
tax and an enlarged emissions trading scheme that will cripple business. This National
Government, supported by ACT and United Fu ture, supports rural communities. The
other side of the Chamber, I am embarrassed to say, does not.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am pleased to rise to take a call on behalf of
New Zealand First. It is always a delight to follow the Hon Damien O’Connor and to
echo many of his sentiments during this Co mmittee of the whole House stage. Looking
at my notes, I see I have made mention of  the Committee of the “whole Hose” rather
than of the “whole House”, and I think this t ypo is rather apt given that a hose is turned
on at the tap. And opening the taps is what this Government appears hell-bent on doing
when it comes to biosecurity risks facing Ne w Zealand and its appa rent willingness to
allow them access.
This Government—this National-led ad ministration—by its own admission accepts
and acknowledges that the agricultural sector  is the cornerstone of New Zealand’s
economy. Three dollars out of ev ery four that this country earns in foreign exchange
come ultimately from things that we grow a nd things that we harvest—farming, fishing,
forestry, the sheep farms, the beef farms, the vineyards, the orchards, the market
gardeners, the agriculture industry, mussel farming, salmon, and pl antation forests. We
have trees for Africa in this  country, and we harvest and replant them for timber and
particle boards, pulp and paper, and even logs.

items.speaker: Then there is the jewel in the crown
items.text: the dairy industry. New Zealand’s dairy farmers
are the best in the world and their cows really are cash cows. One dollar in every four of
this country’s export earnings—fully one -third of the $3 mentioned earlier—is
generated by hard-working and under-appreciat ed dairy cockies. One-third of all cross-
border trade in dairy products globally eman ates from New Zealand, as does $3 out of
every $4 that this country ha s to spend on cars, and aerop lanes, and televisions, and
medicines, and X-ray machines, and medical  isotopes, and magnetic resonance imaging
scanners, and computers, and cell phones, and microphones like this one, and all the
other things that we have to import from overseas because we cannot or do not make
them here. Three out of every four of the dollars we have to spend on those things
comes from agriculture, and one of thos e dollars—one-third of agriculture’s
contribution—comes from dairy, the much-mali gned dairy sector, the sector that gets
called dirty.

MINIMUM WAGE (STARTING-OUT WAGE) AMENDMENT BILL
In Committee
Part 1  Amendments to principal Act

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I am privileged to be th e first to stand, from the
Labour Opposition, to strongly oppose the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill. I want to start by just reminding listeners and the people who have
taken a great interest in this debate exactly  what this bill does. What this bill does is
return us to youth ra tes of a kind we have not seen since last centu ry. For 16 and 17-
year-olds starting out in their first job, they can be employed on 80 percent of the
minimum wage. Fair enough, you may say. But the pr oblem with this bill is that if they
go on to another job while they are still 16 or 17, they can be employed on 80 percent of
the minimum wage again and again and agai n. So the experience that they gain as
young workers—even leading up to their time  of being 16—at th e age of 16 and 17
counts for nothing if they leave their job and go on to another job, if they are fired under
the 90-day no-rights bill, and if there is no reason given, as there does not have to be
under this Government’s handiwork.
What it means is that it is basically a revolving door youth rate. It is not a starting-out
youth rate. If the Government were serious a bout starting out, it w ould have stuck with
the provisions that were already in the bill that apply to only 16 and 17-year-olds for 3
months or 200 hours, whichever is the greate r. That applies only once. So all of the
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8623
arguments that have been put across the House about how this gives a young worker a
chance, how they need to have time to ga in experience, and so on are just rubbish
because no one can convince me that someone  who works for 6 months in a job at 80
percent of the adult wage, at $11 an hour, does not gain experience and then deserves to
have their pay cut if they move on to another job.
We want, and the Government says it wants, to see 16 and 17-year-olds in study. We
want to see them at school, at polytech, at university, or in apprenticeships. The
National Party says that is what it wants to se e. If that is the case, many of them will be
working part-time in part-time jobs. So they  will have a job in the holidays in between
times. They will have a job after work, perhap s. But those jobs will be jobs that often
are temporary, that do not ca rry on for 6 months, and so  those people, those young
people who are trying to get ahead by studying, will be in the situation where every time
they start a new job while they are 16 and 17, they are going to have go back down the
ladder to 80 percent of the adult wage.
The second thing this bill does is bri ng back youth rates for 18 and 19-year-olds,
which we have not seen in New Zealand sin ce last century. We have not seen them in
New Zealand since last century. What this bi ll means is that 18 and 19-year-olds who
have been on a social security benefit for 6 months can be punish ed for having been on
a benefit by being able to be employed at 80 percent of the a dult wage. We are not
talking about just unemployed young New Zealanders. By the way, I need to correct Mr
Banks, and I will have some other things to say about his contribution the other day. But
he was talking about young New Zealanders of 15 on the dole—15 and 16. They do not
get the dole. They do not get the dole. Social  security benefits in this bill cover the
whole gamut of them all, including the unemplo yment benefit, but al so things like the
invalids benefit, the sickness benefit, and—what is it called, Jacinda?

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: The independent youth benefit.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: The independent youth benefit. It covers all of those, and also
young parents who are 18 and 19. So they will ha ve been on a social security benefit.
They drag themselves up to Work and Income , get offered a job, and it is at 80 percent
of the adult wage. They say, under this bill: “Oh, I’m sorry, Work and Income. I cannot
manage on 80 percent. I can’t manage on $11 an  hour.” But what this bill will allow is
that if Work and Income has deemed that job to be satisfactory on its terms—and we all
know how tough it has become recently, how unfriendly, and what an awful experience
it is for so many people—it can then say to that 18 or 19-year-old: “Well, I’m really
sorry, but you have to have a stand-down of 13 weeks.” So they get doubly punished—
first of all, by dragging themselves off a be nefit. Most of them will have been on a
social security benefit through no fault of th eir own. They will have tried hard to get a
job. They apply for a job, and when an 18 or 19- year-old says that they cannot afford to
live on $11 an hour and they want to look for something else, they get told by Work and
Income that they are being sanctioned a nd they are going to be punished by having a
stand-down for 13 weeks.
There are other issues around this bill that  have not been answered, and were not
answered satisfactorily in the Transport a nd Industrial Relations  Committee. There are
all the issues around discrimination for young people, and I will put those aside for now
and come back to them, perhaps, later in the debate. But on the issue of work
discrimination, discrimination on the basis of  employment, there is  very strong advice
from the Human Rights Commission that em ployers should not discriminate against
people on the basis of their employment status—in other words, if they have been or are
on a social security benefit.
What I think this Government is doing is leading employers down the garden path to
believing that when someone comes to apply for a job, an 18 or 19-year-old, they will
8624 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
be able to ask them whether they are on a soci al security benefit. They will be able to
ask them that because they want to be ab le to offer them 80 percent of the adult
minimum wage—in other words, $11 an hour—a nd then they are able to discriminate
against those workers because they are able  to find out the information and then the
worker can say: “Well, I’m sorry, but I don’ t want the job.”, or the employer can say:
“Well, I’m sorry, I don’t want you, because we don’t want people who have been on a
benefit.” There are real privacy  issues involved in this that  have not been satisfactorily
answered.
My question to the Minister in the chair is  why we are doing this. Well, I think we
know the answer to that. The answer is that the National Government has no ideas about
how to address our crisis in youth unempl oyment. Two years ago David Bennett, that
member over there, stood up in this Hous e and passionately opposed youth rates. There
is a bookload of quotes from him about how they were inappropriate, and I am looking
forward to reciting them. We even heard fr om Simon O’Connor some quotes from the
Catholic Church. I know the Catholic Church talks about the dignity of work and about
respect, and the dignity is about the way people are treate d and how they are rewarded
for their work. It is not about just having a job.
Simon O’Connor: It was Mr Little who was quo ting Pope Francis—your colleague
behind you, the one smiling. He quoted Pope Francis.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: And you quoted it back, Mr O’Connor—you did.
Simon O’Connor: Rerum Novarum—you should read it.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: Yes, that is right. I have got many. I have read at length the
various encyclicals of instru ction from the Catholic Ch urch, because I have been
engaged in having those debates with the Ca tholic Church about their workers over
many years. But the Catholic Church a nd the church generally does not support the
dignity of work if it means people are not fair ly rewarded for their work, are not fairly
treated, are not able to earn a living, are not  able to build a decent life, and are not
treated with respect. That is what this bill does.
The other excuse is that this is someho w going to create jobs. That is the other
excuse. As my colleague Andrew Little has so rightly pointed out, cutting wages does
not create jobs. There are no jobs unless there is work to  be done. Employers do not
take people on as some kind of beneficiary. They do not do it out of the kindness of
their hearts. They do it because there is work to be done. And the workers who come
along and do that work have a right to be  respected and paid properly, rewarded
properly, for the work they do.
This bill not only will impact on 16 to 19- year-olds but also will impact on older
workers. I have had many of them express concern to me about creating a market of
young workers who are cheaper, who are on $11 an hour, and who will displace older
workers. Indeed, that has happened in the past.
The worst thing about this bill is that we  have tried these methods before in New
Zealand. This is not a new idea. In fact, it is  a very, very old National Party idea. It is a
very old ACT Party idea that if you cut young workers’ wages, it cr eates jobs. Just go
back to the last time we had real youth rates in this country, in the 1990s. When youth
rates were $4.50 an hour, when people were getting paid $4.50 an hour, we had some of
the highest youth unemployment that we have ev er seen in this count ry. So this bill is
not going to deliver on its stated aims.

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It is an absolute delight to be called, thank you very
much. I spoke on the Minimum Wage (Starting-Out Wage) Amendment Bill on
Thursday last week, and I drew  the attention of the House to my first experience in the
labour market. I outlined the excitement I felt when I went downstairs and my mum had
bought a new Kingfisher Briggs and Stratton lawnmower. It was the first step of my
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8625
becoming self-sufficient and learning to save , and learning the value of work and the
reward one can achieve from work, not just  financial but spiritual, and the dignity
therein.
The next job I had was with Mr Brown on his milk round. We would get up at about
4.30 in the morning—and I must say, it is no easier getting up at 4.30 in the morning
now than it was then—meet up with the truck, and then we would get the trolleys out,
load them up with the crates  and the bottles in the crates , and we would hurtle around
the streets of Westown picking up tokens from the bottles, money sometimes, and
delivering them for the full bottles. I must sa y I have a certain am ount of nostalgia for
the fact that we no longer get milk at our front gate, but there we go.
It is all about the dignity of work and th is is what the Minimum Wage (Starting-Out
Wage) Amendment Bill is all about. It  is about giving young people—young people
who may be entering the workforce for the firs t time, lacking skills, lacking experience,
or may be coming off a benefit, or unde rtaking an industry training course—an
opportunity to get the foot on the rung of the employment ladder. It is an opportunity for
them to get their feet on the rung of the employment ladder. This is the ages of 16 to 19.
Why are we doing this? We are creating an  environment that encourages economic
growth, more jobs, and higher wages. We know  that there is a plethora of research,
particularly from the UK, about the benefits of work, the health benefits of work. There
are a number of studies that have come out s howing that work is extremely beneficial to
one’s physical health and one’s mental health. Work is good for health.
We know that long-term periods of unemplo yment lead to a host of bad outcomes,
and where better to intervene but with our young people. This is why we believe that the
Minimum Wage (Starting-Out Wage) Ame ndment Bill is a very good piece of
legislation. It is very interesting that La bour replaced the youth minimum wage with a
so-called new entrants wage—that reminds one a little bit of infant school, does it not—
which provided the same rate of pay as the starting-out wage. You may think that that is
interesting and ask why Labour members are opposing it now.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: For how long?

items.speaker: Dr CAM CALDER
items.text: It lasted for 3 months, in answer to your question, or 200
cumulative hours. The feedback we have had from employers is that it was not long
enough, that it is too complicat ed, impractical, and the 3-mont h period is too short. So,
apparently, feedback from employers suggest s they need to calculate a new worker’s
entire work history on the new entrants wage  before hiring them under its conditions.
How many do we think use it? Very, very few. So although Labour’s policy provides
the same rate of pay as the starting-out wa ge, the conditions are unw orkable, virtually,
and unattractive for not only the employers but the employees.
Just to recapitulate, the starting-out wage will be set at 80 percent of the minimum
wage, and it is available for 16 to 17-year-olds in their first 6 months of work with a
new employer; 18 and 19-year-olds can also bene fit from this starting-out wage if they
are coming directly off the benefit that th ey have been receiving for 6 continuous
months; also the benefits can apply to 16 to 19-year-olds in training in a recognised
industry training course involvi ng at least 40 credits  a year. This is a reduction, as you
may recall, of 20 credits from the current scheme.
So it is a very good piece of legislation. What is its possible sequelae? Well, the
Ministry of Business, Innovatio n and Employment suggests that the starting-out wage
could create up to 2,000 new jobs for 16 to 19-years-olds in the next 2 years.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: What a typical approach by this
Government. It has got a problem with youth unemployment. We know why it has got a
problem with youth unemployment. It is becau se it has got no visi on for growing the
New Zealand economy. John Key, who decrie d 25,000 teenagers being out of work in
8626 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
2008, his big achievement has been to increase the rate of youth unemployment by a
further 5,000—to 30,000. If you take the people who are 20 to 24 years old, make that
another 90,000 young people out of work. And what is this Government’s answer?
What is its vision to deal with unemployment?  Its vision is to cut the starting rate for 16
and 17-year-olds and some 18 and 19-year-o lds by 20 percent. You know what these
people in the National Pa rty are proposing. They ar e proposing that young people
working at the same rate, with the same productivity, doing exactly the same job in
exactly the same way as an older person can be paid $11 an hour—$11 an hour!
Simon O’Connor: So experience means nothing?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: That is not even enough for the member over there to pay for his
gin and tonic at a local bar, and he wa nts young people to live on $11. Why, I want to
know from that member, should a teenager making hamburgers in the same way at the
same rate with the same efficiency as a 25- year-old be paid a whole lot less? Will that
create new jobs? No, it will not. The evidence is there that it will simply displace older
workers who are currently do ing the job. So the poor guy, or woman, who is older and
working, making those hamburgers, is not goi ng to have a chance, because the boss is
going to sack them or not employ them in the first place in order to  get cheap labour at
$11 an hour—$11 an hour!
Will this work? Well, let me quote the authority, the Minister for Social
Development, if you can call her an authority. She opposed youth rates just 2 years ago.

items.speaker: This is what she said
items.text: “we are not convinced it would reduce youth unemployment, plus
it would be a distraction from the really important work of improving productivity and
growing the economy in order to create long-term jobs, which will keep young people
in New Zealand.” That is what Paula Benne tt, Minister for Social Development, was
saying 2 years ago about Roger Douglas’ bill. So what is with the change in mind? And

items.speaker: Jackie Blue
items.text: “National has not seen any ev idence to show that young people are losing
their jobs because of youth rates. We are not convinced that this bill will reduce youth
unemployment.” How is that for hypocrisy: against youth rates one day, and for them
the next? And why are National members for th em? It is because they have run out of
ideas. They have no vision for New Zealand other than it being a low-wage economy.
What is the problem with New Zealand? Why did we lose 53,000 New Zealanders to
Australia last year? It was because the jobs are not in New Zealand and because we
have low wages. So this Minimum Wage (S tarting-out Wage) Amendment Bill is a bill
to increase the flow of Kiwis across the Tasm an, so they can put their energy and their
taxation into the Australian economy. This is a Government that has no vision about
creating jobs. This is a Government that has no vision about upskilling New Zealanders
for high-paid jobs. Why is it that the numbe r of apprenticeships is down 20 percent
from when this Government got into offi ce—down 20 percent? Why is it that in one
Budget it slashed $53 million out of the skills training budget? Why is it that in
Christchurch on Sunday, on St Patrick’s Day, the bars were full of Irish workers,
imported to do the work because this Government had no plan to upskill New
Zealanders to rebuild Christchurch? That is an absolute disgrace—an absolute disgrace.
This is not only counterproductive, because  it is not about increasing skills and
increasing jobs, but also unjust and unfair.
What this Government is doing is saying that young people are out of work because
it is their fault, we are paying them too much; not that they are out of work because this
Government has failed utterly in its econom ic management. So what does it say? It
says: “We will put our young people on $11 an hour .” That is a bit rich coming from
those people, the Cabinet Ministers and MPs w ho gave themselves a big fat increase in
income by cutting the tax rates for the top inco me earners. That is unfair. It is not on
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8627
that this is a Government that will reward  the most wealthy peopl e in the country but
will continue to hit the people who are at the bottom of the heap.
Why is it that Lesley Longstone is gett ing $1,000 in severance for each day she
worked—$425,000? That is what it will hand ou t to the people at the top: $425,000 of
New Zealand taxpayer money given to Lesley  Longstone because Hekia Parata could
not get on with her. So it will reward the rich. Why is it that Don Elder, the former chief
executive of Solid Energy, right now retains his salary at a rate of $1.3 million a year
while he is at home doing the garden? The Government will reward the rich, but its
answer is always to cut the income of people at the bottom.
So the brave new world for the National Government is to have our young people
leave school and go out to work at $11 an hour. That will not solve the unemployment
problem amongst young people. They know that . The last speaker from the National
side, Cam Calder, said that the bill will cr eate 2,000 jobs for 16 and 17-year-olds. What
he forgot to tell the Chamber was that it takes 2,000 jobs away from the people who are
20, 25, 35, or 45. This is about job displacemen t. This Government has no ideas about
job creation. It brought in th e Youth Guarantee scheme. That  was going to get lots of
people into jobs. I saw a w ithered pumpkin that was produced under one scheme. This
Government wasted millions of dollars on a scheme it then scrapped. It talks loudly
about the Limited Service Volunteer scheme. Th at has its good aspects, but the truth of
the matter is that 40 percent of the young people going on to that scheme go back on to
the benefit and go back into unemployment.  What this country needs is a genuine
answer for upskilling our young people, so th at we can be an innovative, high-growth,
high-skill, and high-tech econom y. It does not need a Governme nt that says the answer
is to force wages down to $11 an hour, and that is what it is doing.
This Government has no ideas. We had a j ob summit. Remember the jobs that were
going to be created out of that? That was 4 years ago. Where are the jobs? [Interruption]
Let the next National speaker rise up on his or her hind legs and tell us how many jobs
were actually created. Do you know, Mr O’Connor, what the answer is? Fewer than one
in five of what John Key promised. It was a job summit that was about rhetoric. It was
not about creating jobs. Now, in desperat ion, the Government comes to the Chamber
and says: “If there’s youth unemployment it must be the young people’s fault, and we
will hammer them.”
There is one thing in the legislation that I will support, and that is Darien Fenton’s
Supplementary Order Paper 193, which talks about lifting the minimum wage to $15 an
hour. Why would I support that? Because it is  wrong that 40 percent of the kids living
in poverty in this country right now come from working families—40 percent of the
kids living in poverty come from working families. I have got an electorate full of
people where mums and dads take it in tu rns, they do shift work, one goes out during
the day and one goes out at night, and they cannot produce enough income on the
minimum wage they get paid—including clean ing those members’ offices—to have a
living wage.
I grew up in a New Zealand where people said  that if you do an honest week’s work,
you get a living wage for that week. I want one member—one member—of the National
Government to stand up and say why peopl e working hard, doing an honest week’s
work are not entitled to a living wage. I want one member to stand up and say that he or
she could live on $13.75 an hour, which is the minimum wage. It is not a living wage.
Most particularly it is not a living wage in the city that I represen t, Auckland, in Mt
Roskill. That money does not give you enough money to feed your kids properly, to
clothe them, and to give them the opportunities that most other kids have. Why is that at
my low-income schools some of the kids have never got to the beach? They have never
been away on a holiday—that is asking too much. Mum and dad cannot afford even to
8628 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
put shoes on their feet. And this Govern ment says: “We’ll pay them $13.75 an hour—
but, hang on, if you’re a young person we’ll pay you $11 an hour.” How generous!
What a decent Government! What a Government, which can reward itself with big fat
tax cuts, but cannot give people a living wage , and which now says that the answer to
youth unemployment is to cut the wages of those young people doing the same work as
the people next to them—

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I think the previous member, the Hon Phil
Goff, was following the philos ophy that if you say it loud enough it must be true. He
also alluded to the fact that this b ill, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill, is a disgrace. I will tell you, Mr Chair, what is a disgrace.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Do not bring the Chair—

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I am telling you, Mr Chair, what is a disgrace. What is—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: No, no, you must not bring the Chair
into the debate.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I will say to members and also the Chair what is a disgrace, and that
is making members of the Ne w Zealand public beholden to the Government to ensure
that it can make its way to the next election and secure itself a place on the Government
benches. That is what happened across 9 years of the Labour administration.
We have also heard words coming from the other side about punishment and about
discrimination. This is not a disgrace, it is not punishment, and it is not discrimination.
This is about creating opport unity. If you go out there and talk  to employers, they will
tell you that they want to employ young peopl e. But they will also explain that when
you consider the total remuneration of any employee, it is not about just the hourly rate.
It is also about sick leave, it is also about annual leave, and it is also about ACC levies.
When you consider all of that in the mix, th ere are a number of businesses that simply
cannot afford to take on a young person who has low skills and a lack of experience,
and, arguably, there is a disconnect between them and what is required by the employer.
That has cost some 9,000 jobs sin ce 2008, when the youth minimum wage was
removed—over 5 years a 42 percent reduction in the number of 15 to 19-year-olds in
employment. That is what is a disgrace here.
What this bill sets out to do is actually ch allenge that and find the settings that will
marry employers and employees back together , in particular those in the youth area,
who, we know, if they do not find their way at that age into some form of training or
meaningful employment have a very high likelihood at the age of 18 of transitioning on
to an adult benefit and likely staying there for some period of time.
This bill is specifically aimed at ensuring th at employers have the settings that they
need to take a chance on the young person. Cert ainly even yesterday in my constituency
office two people came to me literally pulli ng their hair out, wanting to employ local
people, in particular young people, and give  them a chance. But they cannot get those
young people. They cannot get those young people, because those young people are
disconnected from a work ethic. They ar e disconnected from the sorts of skills—
[Interruption] This is what they are telling me. If those members want to come and sit in
my electorate office and listen to employers  in Northland who want to employ young
people, local people, they will hear this for themse lves. Those young people are
disconnected from what employers need. It is  not that the employers  are not trying to
reach out to them. This bill is about providi ng the appropriate incentives and platform
for employers to seek out those opportun ities with the young people. It is not
compulsory; it is an arrangement between the employer and the employee, and it is over
a 6-month period.
We have heard comments about the fact that  this will displace other workers. Well, I
can also tell you that employers very quick ly identify the value in an employee, and
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8629
those employees are valued by the employer. There is an intrinsic relationship in a
successful business between the employe r and the employee. Good employees who
show initiative, who are given a chance, a nd who demonstrate ability advance their way
through that business. The business relies on good employees. So this is not about
displacing; it is about providi ng opportunity and an entry point. That  is the distinct
difference.
But time and time again we hear, in particul ar from the Labour Party, that this is
about punishment, it is about di scrimination, and it is disgraceful. Well, it is the entire
opposite to those things, because when members here actually take the time to step out
from behind their parliamentar y desks and talk to employees and employers, what they
will find is that it is about providing the opportunity and backing these young people
and giving employers a chance to see whether or not those young people can make the
grade. It then goes to the employee to show  that they can, but they need the chance.
Nine thousand jobs across 5 years is unacceptable.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: We seem to have this attitude that we are a benign
country, that we love our kids, that we w ill help our kids. But, actually, what we are
hearing from this Government and with this bill, the Minimum Wage (Starting-out
Wage) Amendment Bill, is that we will not. What  we are hearing with this bill is that
we think our young people are worth less than ot hers. With this bill we are saying that
young people are worthless. Mr Sabin, who just spoke earlier, actually said that he has
heard that young people have no skills—they have no work skills. Well, if that was the
case, then they would not be employed in the first place—no young person would be—
but they are. They certainly are.
We are not investing in our young people. In these sorts of  circumstances, what we
are trying to do is we are trying to give th em the worst starting-out work experience we
possibly can. We are putting them into places where the employer has an incentive to
employ them, certainly, and to pay them less than any other worker, to pay them at a
wage that they can hardly live on. We are saying that that is OK if we pass this law.
Forcing young people into dead-end jobs just because they have been on a benefit is
designed only to get them off the benefits  so the unemployment statistics look better,
