when we know that the way you address unemployment is to create jobs. This bill is not
going to create jobs. We have s een no evidence of that, and we have seen it in the past
as well. Reducing the wages for young people does not create jobs. There seems to be
no other reason for forcing the wages of  young people down except to make them
cheaper—except to make employers able to exploit them easier.
I find it interesting that we are doing this  to young people. We are focusing on them
having lower wages, but we never ever seem to attack those who are much older who
are also on benefits. When you consider that we  have a universal benefit that is applied
to people over the age of 65, where they ge t 66 percent of the average wage, and that
this Government never attacks that, one has to think why. I suspect that it is because
those who are over 65 are well organised and they tend to vote for this existing
Government, actually.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Not all of them.

items.speaker: DENISE ROCHE
items.text: No, some of them do not. A lot of them vote for New Zealand
First. But if you think about it, young people have as many expenses as older people.
They do not eat less food. They do not use le ss electricity. They do not wear fewer
clothes. They do not pay less for their expens es in transport. They are paying the same,
so why should they be penalised?
Already, 16-year-olds, 17-year-olds, 18-yea r-olds, and 19-year-old s are able to be
paid a training rate. We have already got that in legislation. They can be paid a training
rate for a total of 3 months. This bill does not allow a sensible relationship between an
8630 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
employer and an employee. What it allows is for a worker to be employed at lower rates
for up to 6 months with no guarantee that th ey will continue their employment. Then
they go to the bottom of the scale agai n when they are re-employed by another
employer, if they get another job. This opens up young people to being exploited.
We believe that if we are sensible and if we are se rious about ad dressing youth
unemployment, there is a lot more that we should be doing in terms of education and
investment in youth. There is a lot more we could be doing in terms of training. There is
a lot more that we could be doing in terms of getting them to a point where they are
work-ready. We are not seeing that type of compassionate approach with this
Government. This bill certainly does not go any of the way there.
We believe that the same work should be valued the same. We have been through
this discussion before with women.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: I rise to speak in this Committee stage of the
Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendmen t Bill in the name of the inspirational
Minister of Labour, the Hon Simon Bridges.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Eschatological—we need to get that word in.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Indeed—indeed. We can all agre e that it is important that
young people are given opportunities to engage in  training in their chosen industry, but
it is also important that young people genera lly are given a go. It is the New Zealand
way, for goodness’ sake! But, in respect of the earlier comments that we have heard,
employers have so far indicat ed that they are not using the training minimum wage
created under Labour, and Labour really needs to consider why that might be the case.
We as a Parliament do need to address th e serious issue of youth unemployment. We
would be derelict in our dutie s if we did not. This bill, through the creation of a wage
for 16 to 19-year-olds entering the workfor ce and coming off a benefit—that is the
biggest thing of all—or undert aking an industry training c ourse, will do a great deal
towards giving people a go. Speaking for myself, I have never had to have a benefit, in
terms of an unemployment benefit.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: He could be on a vicar’s stipend.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: No, it is not skiting. It is—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: No, I said a vicar’s stipend. Isn’t that a benefit?

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Oh, I see what you mean. I thought you said I was skiting.
But the reality—and Mr Goff will know, because although I am sure he is not as old as I
am, we have been through various stages of New Zealand life together at the same time.
Certainly when I came to New Zealand as an  immigrant, it was remarkably, well, not
easy to get a job, but there were plenty of  jobs and plenty of opportunities—plenty.
Modern youth is not quite in the same place, so we have to work harder to give them
opportunities.
We also have to provide, as this bill  does, opportunities to encourage employers. I
would have to say that I am disappointed with the expressions of att itude that I hear in
the debate thus far from the Opposition par ties, as if employers are some sort of
dreadful Dickensian characters who ar e going to exploit young people at every
opportunity. That has not been my e xperience in talki ng to employers. [ Interruption]
No, it really is not. When I th ink of the employers whom I meet on a daily basis, from
one end of the West Coast - Tasman electora te to the other, they  are, without doubt,
proud of their staff. They actually like their staff. They have trained them after they
have selected them, they have watched them  develop, and they are extremely pleased to
have the association with them. I would like to remind the House that this starting-out
wage is voluntary. Employers and employees must agree together on whether it will
apply. It will improve a currently flawed system greatly.
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8631
If we do agree—and I hope we can agree on some points—that youth unemployment
levels are far too high, and that there is  a need for young people to gain opportunity,
experience, and reasonable financial compen sation, then why is it that the Opposition
arguments seem to want to match young work ers fresh in vision and enthusiasm but
with briefer curriculum vitaes , less experience, and more po tential risk to the employer
against the older employees whose experience and position are valuable and
entrenched? Or do I see lurking in the mind of Andrew Little the Amalgamated
Engineering, Printing and Manufacturing Un ion banner, which wants to protect the
members of unions against the oncoming workforce that could threaten the jobs there? I
cannot see it. I cannot see why Mr Goff says this  is a displacement exercise to get rid of
older and experienced workers and bring in young ones.

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Because that’s the experience in the past.

items.speaker: CHRIS AUCHINVOLE
items.text: Well, I do not see it. I cannot imagine it happening to any
great extent. There might be the odd one. But the same apprehension was voiced by
Labour when we introduced the—

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: You know, the most disappointing thing about that
speech from Chris Auchinvole is that at th e end of last week thousands of young gay
men and women who had never before hear d of him were uttering the name Chris
Auchinvole as somebody who had offered a progressive vision. This was a member
who, unbeknownst to him, had trended on Twitter, when he did not even know what
that meant, because of such a fantastic address that he gave. He gave hope to many
young people in this country last week. And now he has shattered the illusion, because
now we have seen the truth.
If there is one thing that this bill,  the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill, does, it is th at it very accurately and very emphatically explains the
difference between the National Party on the one hand and the Labour Party on the
other. National is a party that does not recognise the opportunity for exploitation when it
sees it, does not see it in the laws that  it enacts and creates, and does not understand
how the labour market in this country and, indeed, most free count ries properly works.
It does not understand that changing laws does not create work, and does not understand
that to create work of value—of value not  only to the employer but to the worker—it
needs active investment, understanding, and innovation. It does not happen when you
cheapen the price of labour, and there is only one thing that this bill will do, and that is
cheapen the price of labour. It so happens th at it will cheapen the price of the most
vulnerable labour, our youngest and the new en trants to our workforce, and those who
have had difficulty finding work and who even at their tender teenage years have
perhaps had a period in the workforce then out of it for a 6-mont h or longer period and
are then trying to get back into it. They are the ones who will be badly affected.
It will not create work. Phil Goff is absolutely correct. Measures like this do not
create work. What it does is give an opportunity to employers to say: “Aha! Here we go.
I don’t have to pay $13.75. I can get away with $11.80.” or whatever it is.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Eleven dollars. It is no t even $11.80—$11. “I can get away
with paying even less, so I will.” Actually, that is the way many employers think. If Mr
Auchinvole is right when he asks why empl oyers would do this, because they value
their workers—well, they will not be looking to this law. The good employers in this
country do not look at laws like this, because they respect working people—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: It’s an option; it’s not compulsory.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: —they want to pay the best, a nd they want to do the best. But
there are employers—and it might be a surp rise to Mr Sabin to know this—who will
work at the edges of the law because they know  they can get away with it. That is how
8632 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
they run their businesses, and that is the nature of their business. They are marginal
businesses of low value, and they do not actually value the work people do. It may
come as a surprise but there are employers like that. I know. I have met them. I met one
of them once with Max Bradford, just afte r the Employment Contracts Act was passed.
Max Bradford was shocked to find that there was an employer who told a young worker
that he would sign him up on an apprenticeship if he could pay him $50 a week. I might
remind members that even in 1993, $50 a week was an absolutely paltry sum. This
young worker never got his apprenticeship, ne ver got his training, but was paid $50 a
week. When Max Bradford found out about that  employer with me, we visited him. He
was absolutely shocked. There are employers like that. They will exploit this law, and
they will make it worse.
This law will do no good. It will do no good for working people—young working
people. It will actually do no good for the labour market, at all. It will do no good for
the good employers who are looking for good young people and who want to offer them
the best but who are compe ting with the exploitative,  the underminers, and the
employers who have nothing to offer. That is the National Party approach. It is not
interested in creating work. It is interested in reducing the cost of labour, because that is
what its mates tell it they want. That is what its mates tell it they want. They said:
“Make it easier for us. We will employ young people. Just make it cheaper for us.”
Actually, the truth is that the people who talk like that and who talk to their National
Party mates in Parliament are not interested in young people. They are interested just in
getting a job done as cheaply as possible, and that is what this bill will do. That is why
we are opposed to it. That is why we will support Darien Fenton’s Supplementary Order
Papers to provide for a minimum wage of $15 and to at least take  the 18 and 19-year-
olds out of it, because by that time, if you ar e not fit for school, if you are trying to look
for something different and you are in th e workforce, why—by the time you get to 18
and 19—should you go backwards?

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: Labour is opposed to this bill, the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, and fo r all the right reasons. From the Labour
Party’s perspective, the visi on we have for New Zealand is a high-wage, high-skill
economy, not this race to the bottom that is promoted by this bill by that Government.
The front page of the Waikato Times yesterday, I think, said it all, with its big banner
headline “Jobless fight for work”. That wa s the headline on the front page of the
Waikato Times yesterday, and in there it documen ted the very real world—not the
pretend one that we hear about  from the other side, from the Government, but what is
actually going on out there. The Waikato Times  documented that in Hamilton the
Earthquake Commission has advertised 120 j obs at the Hamilton office since it opened
last year. One thousand and thirteen people have applied for those 120 jobs. At the
burger chain Wendy’s, which is moving into Hamilton shortly, it had 100 applications
for just six management positions, and it is expecting to have 500 or more people apply
for just 50 minimum wage crew jobs. Th e Mexico Group is moving into Hamilton.
These are not exciting jobs, by the way. This is not the brighter future that that
Government promised. These are all minimum wage jobs. Two hundred people had
applied for 25 jobs at that restaurant in Hamilton. That restaurant is going to be opening
next month.
That is the real position that is happe ning out there. Small numbers of minimum
wage jobs are becoming available, and larg e numbers of people ar e lining up for them.
It is in that environment that this National Government decides that the best thing to do
for the future for New Zealand is to lower wages, and to lower wages for 15 to 19-year-
olds because it does not believe in that group. The Government has actually given up on
15 to 19-year-olds. It has given up on them in terms of their being able to do a good job
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8633
at a decent rate of pay. What this bill says is that the Government does not believe that
those people, those 15 to 19-year-olds, are up to a decent wage. It believes that those
people need to have a law put in  place that actually lowers their wages so that they can
get an opportunity. It does not believe in young people.
Government members have also given up on arguing, as they did ju st last week in
this House, that this bill creates jobs. Of c ourse, it is ridiculous for them to even have
pretended—as the Minister of Labour, Simon Br idges, did last week—that this piece of
legislation somehow creates jobs. In fact, it does the opposite. I want  to go through that
so that people understand why it does the opposite. When wages are lowered, spending
power in our communities is actually di minished. When spending power in our
communities is diminished, that actually means fewer jobs, not more—fewer jobs—
because jobs are created by work, not by cutting wages.
Jobs are created when there is work to be done, because employers are not charitable
organisations, as Mike Sabin would have us believe. They are not going to just go out
there and employ people when there is no work to do. Those employers who were
supposedly sitting in his electorate office last  week were not there saying: “Mike, I’ve
got no work that needs to be done, but I woul d just really love to employ some young
people to put some money in their pockets.”

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Trust me—they’ve got the work.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: That is not what they were there saying. They were not there
saying that, at all. They were saying: “I’v e got work to do and I want to employ the
cheapest people possible.” That is what they wanted from that member.
The work is there. This legislation will not create one extra job. What it will do is
lower wages. I warned New Zealanders last week, and I will warn them again, if they
think that the lower wages agenda from that  National Government is just going to be
targeted at young workers, they need to thi nk again. This is the slippery slope. This is
where lower wages start, but it is not where they stop. In this environment, which I just
described before—that situation happening in Hamilton where there is a small number
of minimum wage jobs available and larg e numbers of desperate unemployed people
going for those jobs—it is a haven for employers if they wish to exploit people, because
that gives the employer all the cards. They hold all the cards in that situation.
I want to go through—for the benefit of the members opposite, because they do not
seem to get this—the reality of what actually  happens in this scenario. Mike Sabin and

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole both said
items.text: “O h, look, it’s all righ t because it will  be voluntary.”
Voluntary for whom? I will go back to th e burger chain Wendy’s. There were 100
applications for six jobs. What is going to happen in that situation? Let us apply this bill
to that situation. The Wendy’s chain manager decides that they want to employ a person
who is, let us say for argument’s sake, an 18- year-old, and they fit the criteria set down
in this bill. Is that Wendy’s burger chain manager really going to  say to that young
person: “Look, by law I can pay you as low as $11 an hour. Would you like that, or
would you really rather be pa id at $13.75 an hour? Your ch oice. You choose. You tell
me.” Do members opposite really believe that that is the discussion that is going to
happen when Wendy’s fills those six jobs that  those 100 people applied for? They have
all gone quiet opposite because th ey know the real answer. The real answer is that the
Wendy’s burger chain manager is  going to say: “Eleven dolla rs—take it or leave it.”.
Take it or leave it.
That is what the National Government believ es is a voluntary situation. They believe
that that is giving freedom of choice—remember that from Bill Birch—to that 18-year-
old, because they will be able to say: “No. Thanks very much, but I’ll just leave your
job.” They will have stood in that queue of  100 people, and, mysteriously, the National
Government members opposite believe that th ey are going to voluntarily say no to that
8634 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
job because they will not accept $11 an hou r. That, by anyone else’s standards, is
compulsory. It is not giving freedom of choi ce to those young people, and it is certainly
not going to bring about the high-wage, high-skill economy that we need to get this
economy going. That is what we need in this  country, not these endless bad pieces of
legislation that this Government keeps br inging forward, which actually get us in a
downward economic spiral.
This is yet another piece of legislation that will actually take our economy down. It
will be felt in the regions. It will be felt in the provincial cities like Hamilton, where
those jobs—that small number of jobs—are driving those very l ong queues. And in
those very long queues there will be people from a range of age groups. Andrew Little
is right: it will be the bad employers who take advantage of this. The good employers do
not need this legislation. They do not want  this legislation, because they will be
prepared to pay a decent wage for a decent day’s work.
What this bill is encouraging employers to  do is to go below a decent wage. In New
Zealand we have already determined that. The Government, actually, has determined
what it thinks a minimum wage is. It th inks it is $17—$13.75. Gosh, I wish it was $17,
but it thinks it is $13.75. It th inks that is a minimum wage. But when it comes to young
people, it does not think they are worth even  that. It thinks that  they should not be
getting a decent wage for a decent day’s work. That is fundamental to what I understand
to be the sort of fairness th at most Kiwis believe is right in this country—a fair day’s
pay for a fair day’s work. This bill is undermin ing that very sacred Kiwi value. It is
coming from the National Government because it has always come from the National
Government. It has always been its soluti on. It does not matte r what part of the
economic cycle we are in—recession or not—whenever there has been a National
Government in place—

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora. Thank you, Mr Chai r. I rise to take a call
on the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Am endment Bill. I will address a couple of
issues that Mr Sabin and Mr Auchinvole raised.
First of all, Mr Sabin with the story that he graced us with in regard to employers
coming to see him to say that they were unable to employ young people with the skills
that they required to gain employment in side their industry. I recognise Mr Sabin’s
point. I recognise the point s of those employers. Ho wever, his answer—this
Government’s answer—is completely misguide d. If this Government truly wanted to
support those local employers to employ lo cal young people, then why would it have
removed the funding from places like Ōtorohanga, where you have a massively
successful model, where the community has come together to train local young people
with local skills for local employment, where the Mayor of Ōtorohanga has brought
together those employers and said: “What ar e the skills you need, guys? What are the
skills we need for our young people to actually be able to get out there and gain work
just down the road from where they live?” . That is what happened. Employers came in
and they highlighted—in this instance, in th e Wintec prospectus—which of those skills
were the ones that were needed. Local gove rnment worked with Wintec and said: “We
will give you a building with zero rent—zer o rent—so that you can actually come here
and train our young people in only the skills that will gain them employment.” That is
something that would actually work, not paying somebody less to do the work. Where is
the incentive for young people? I ask Mr Sa bin how many 16, 17, 18 and 19-year-olds
he has consulted in his constituency about this policy, which he stands by and says is
the answer for us.
I also want to pick up on the comments made by Mr Auchinvole. I am not sure
whether Mr Auchinvole was here in the count ry in the 1990s—whether he was here the
last time we had a youth wage actually put into place. I am not sure whether Mr
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8635
Auchinvole is aware of the statistics around what happened the last time a youth wage
was brought into this country, and the displa cement that Mr Goff talked about. I can
send to Mr Auchinvole’s office some of the suicide statistics for older males from about
that time, when they were laid off th rough the recession, when they found their
companies and employers going into receiver ship and they were trying to pay their
mortgages. They were trying to feed their children, and they could not get a job at the
local gas station pumping gas because they were undercut every single time by a young
person who could be paid le ss. Those are real statistic s. I can send them to Mr
Auchinvole’s office if he would like them. This is going to create the same difficulty,
and it will create no more jobs.
Recently the Ministry of Social Deve lopment and the Minister for Social
Development pulled back funding from  the community answers around youth
employment into major centralisation, partic ularly inside of Auckland, with only four
deliverers. Again, we have been  down this pathway before. It  is not a new idea. It was
not a good idea then, and it is not a good idea now. We have young people who need to
be able to support themselves , particularly at age 18 and 19, yet we are going to put
them on something that none of us in this House would work for. None of us would take
that job, yet we say to them “You will.”, and we have combined it with some legislation
inside the social development portfolio that will force them to do so. To have the word
“choice” used at any time around this issu e, when speaking to 16, 17, 18, and 19-year-
olds, is a fallacy. I would say again, Mr  Sabin: how many 16, 17, 18, and 19-year-olds
have you spoken to? I would suggest very few, Mr Sabin.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Well, I’ve got plenty of young constituents I’ve talked to, actually.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Well, that would be lovely, Mr Sabin. Go out into your
schools. Go out into the schools up there, Mr Sabin, and let us see, when they actually
get the vote, whether they would keep you ther e. These are the voters of the future. The
fact that you will pass this legislation be fore these young people have any way, shape,
or form to either keep you in office or take  you out of office is disr espectful. This is a
group of people who are without power inside  this legislative chamber, and we are
taking advantage of them. Your party is taking advantage of them—

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I am happy to carry on from the
previous speaker, Tracey Martin, and to res pond to some of the calls from members on
the other side talking about how they talk to young people and how their constituents
are unemployed. One of the things that Chris Auchinvole outlined very well is that there
is something that we can all agree on in te rms of this legislation, the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, and that is that we have a massive problem with
youth unemployment. It is actually really good to hear National finally admit to that
point, because we have been saying it for many y ears, that we are at a crisis point when
it comes to our young people and their ability  to find work. What we have had from
members on the opposite side of the Chamber this afternoon are cr ocodile tears around
the rates of youth unemployment, and talking about the lack of engagement of young
people.
But this bill is the only solution they ha ve got to put up. Slashing young people’s
wages is not a solution to youth unemployment. It will accomplish absolutely nothing.
What we are having, as my colleague Sue Mo roney pointed out in her very fine speech,
are members opposite give up on even advancing the arguments that this legislation will
do anything to create jobs. Instead, what we are having are members falling back on
telling us: “Don’t worry, employers do not ha ve to do it.” This is their one great
solution, and they are reassuri ng the nation that it is OK, th at it is voluntary, and that
employers will not have to do it. It is just ridi culous that this is all they have got when
we are at a time of national crisis in terms of youth unemployment. We have 90,000
8636 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
young New Zealanders who are not in any form of education, employment, or training,
and the best that Government members ha ve got is voluntary wa ge slashing as a
solution to it. It is absolutely no wonder that  the Salvation Army gave this Government
a D—a fail—in its recent repo rt when it came to youth unemp loyment and its ability to
deal with this pressing national problem.
This is a Government that is failing. This is a Government that has absolutely
nothing to offer on what we have, which is a crisis point of massively high rates of
unemployment in New Zealand. Forty-five percent of these people are aged between 15
and 24. The unemployment rate for 15 to 19-ye ar-olds is 30.9 percent. We are getting
up there with the worst countries in Eu rope in terms of this age group and
unemployment. This is not something that we can sit back on and say “Well, this is all
we’ve got, but, don’t worry, you don’t really have to do it. It is only a voluntary piece of
legislation anyway.” Youth unemployment is at a point where it requires a real solution.
It is not only we on this side of the Cham ber who believe this. It is quite interesting
to read back over National members’ commen ts in previous debate s on this question in
this Chamber. If we go back to Paula Bennett in March 2010, she said, in response to an
oral question: “we are not convinced it would reduce youth  unemployment, plus it
would be a distraction from the really im portant work of improving productivity and
growing the economy in order to create long-term jobs, which will keep young people
in New Zealand.” Fine words, Ms Bennett. We agree with you entirely.
Then we come to the chair of the select  committee that heard submissions on this
bill, the Transport and Industrial Relations  Committee. There were 61 submissions, and
54 of those were opposed—

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: There were 531, but overwhelmingly—

items.speaker: Darien Fenton
items.text: Only nine in favour.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: Only nine out of all thos e submissions—thank you, Darien
Fenton—were in favour. But if we listen to wh at the chair of that select committee,
David Bennett, has previously said on the ability of youth rates to address this real crisis
we have in New Zealand, he says: “We s hould be promoting to them”—that being
young people—“the need to get education and training, not encouraging them to take
the easy option of temporary employment, which may provide some financial gain at an
early age, but will not deliver long-term be nefits for them as we go forward as a
country.” Then we had David Bennett again in  April 2010: “It is im portant that we do
not set the bar too low, in the sense that our young people who work hard must not find
that they get no reward for their efforts.” We ll, these are fine words from the chair of
the select committee from only 3 years ago. It would be great to hear him address some
of these matters more fully on this, and to take a call and address some of these matters,
because the fact of the matter is that we have  a Government that has done very little. In
fact, it has done nothing, and it has got a fail mark.
We had money set aside in 2011 by this Government to train young New Zealanders.
In November last year only $8 million of that Skills for Canterbury money had been
spent. We lost two crucial years of traini ng our young people to work  in the rebuild of
Canterbury, and what do we see now? We see Christchurch being flooded with migrants
coming in to do that work instead of our  own young people being 2 years into their
training. We have a Government that is not committed. It is not backing education
throughout New Zealand. We have rural polytechnics all over this country that are in
real danger. Taking away the foundation-cour se funding from them has made many of
our polytechnics be in a precarious state. Labour knows that if we are going to address
this real and pressing issue of youth unemployment, where 45 percent of all those who
are unemployed in New Zealand are youth, and where we have youth unemployment
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8637
rates of 30 percent, then we have to do so mething other than offer voluntary legislation
in terms of slashing wages. We have to do so mething to create jobs, and that is what
Labour is committed to doing. Labour is committed to being a hands-on Government
that will get out there, that will back young New Zealanders, and that will say to young

items.speaker: New Zealanders
items.text: “You have a future in this country, and you can stay here.”
In September last year we had the Prime Minister make this great announcement
about how he was going to write personally to  175 employers and ask them to take on
the graduates of the Limited Service Vol unteer scheme, where we have only an 80
percent completion rate. We have very lo w completion rates on the Limited Service
Volunteer courses anyway, but the Prime Mini ster made grand gestures. I think there
were some unemployment figures released around the time, and the Prime Minister
wanted to be seen to be doing something. The Prime Minister promised to keep doing
this—to follow up. As of the beginning of February this year he had not done one
further thing on this. The Prime Minister  had not followed through on his commitment
to young New Zealanders. He had written to zero further employers, asking them to take
on the graduates of our Limited Service Volunteer courses.
This all just goes to show that this is a Government that has no solutions when it
comes to our young people. It has no solutions to tackle the real thing. All we have is
insidious legislation that is intent only on cutting wages.  It is asking our young people
to live on not even the minimum wage or a living wage—it is below that. We are at a
point in our history when we are debati ng what it takes someone to live on. We are
talking about $18.40 an hour and we are asking that our you ng people get paid $11 an
hour. This is not the kind of New Zeala nd that Labour wants to offer to young New
Zealanders. Labour wants to offer young New Zealanders a real reason to stay here, and
slashing the wages of young people will do noth ing to create employment. Government
members opposite have even themselves given up on that argument. We have not heard
it today, and all we are hearin g is a chorus of “Oh, don’t worry. It’s only voluntary.”
They do not believe in their own legislati on. They know it is not going to work and all
they have got to offer now is to tell us “Don’t worry, not all employers will need to do
it.” Labour is not supporting this legislation. It is opposed to it. We  want to see real
solutions to the very real problem of yout h unemployment, not legislation like this
coming before this House.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: Some of the arguments have been
brought out very clearly by the Opposition as  to why this bill, the Minimum Wage
(Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, should not proceed. I think the critical argument
is that this bill is a bill with a low- wage vision for New Zealand, when any New
Zealander knows that our fu ture depends on being high-s killed, high-waged, and high-
tech. This idea that we can compete with the world by continuing to slash the wages that
we pay to our people is absolutely discredited—absolutely discredited.
I tell the members opposite to read what the departmental re gulatory impact
statement says about this bill. This is wh at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and
Employment advised the Minister of Labour. The first thing it advised the Minister was
that it had not considered the options. Why had it not considered the options? Because
the Minister had said: “This is what you are going to do.” So the ministry says right up
front: “This might not be the best way to go, but we have no choice. This is what the
Minister insisted on.” Then it says that, on ba lance, it thinks that “the proposed starting
out wage will have positive employment imp acts for the targeted groups.” What it says
later on is that the targeted group might s ee a little bit of job creation—maybe a few
hundred—but that will be at the expense of  other groups, which will be displaced. It
says that quite explicitly. That is likely to mean, in particular, that some 18 and 19-year-
olds without much work experience and pe ople aged 20 and over and on a benefit may
8638 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
be less attractive to employers than the 16- year-olds or 17-year-olds on the starting-out
wage. So you try to address the problem with unemployed 16-year-olds and 17-year-
olds by making more 18, 19, and 20-year-olds unemployed.
Then there is the Ministry of Education. Wh at does that ministry say about this bill?
It says that it is not the right thing to do, that it is not consistent with the goal of getting
more young people to stay at school to increase  their skills, and that it is encouraging
unskilled young people to drop out of school and to go into a job that they will get
because they are paid peanuts. We do not  need more unskilled 16 and 17-year-olds
leaving school to go into the workforce. We  need more 16 and 17-year-olds staying at
school and improving their educational qualifications.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Come on, Phil, it’s not an election campaign.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: We need more young people to ge t skilled trades, and I put it to
Mr Bennett—oh, I am very glad to see Mr  Bennett here. Let me remind Mr Bennett
what he said about this bill when it was in Roger Douglas’ name. David Bennett said on
21 April 2010—not even 3 years ago; Mr Be nnett, remember this—“The fundamental
proposition this bill puts up is that we need to  pay people less to get them in their first
job so that they can have an unskilled future.” Mr Benne tt, is that what you said—
really? And you went on to say: “That is wh at this bill essentially will do to New
Zealanders. We see a different future for New Zealanders. We want those young people
to get into training and skills so that they are not talking about getting the lowest-paid
job they possibly can, but instead they are l ooking to get the best-paid job they possibly
can.” Mr Bennett, you were right then and you are wrong now. You could not be more
wrong.

items.speaker: I say this to the Government
items.text: what about Labour’s suggestion? We know that we are
short of skilled tradespeople. We do not have  the people to rebuild Christchurch. We do
not have the people who will be needed if a Government ever had the imaginative
policy of creating more houses in Auckland. What we need to do is get young people
off the dole and into skilled training, and what better way than what Labour was
proposing at the last election: to actually pa y the first year’s unemployment benefit to
the employer in order to encourage the employer to take on additional apprentices? Get
more young people into genuine skilled opportunities. Get more people into
apprenticeships, not, Mr Bennett, slash appren ticeships by 20 percent,  as this National
Government has done, and not, as this Government has done, cut $53 million out of
skilled training two Budgets ago, when what we actually need is for more young people
to have skills to contribute to this country.
Do you know what a low-wage vision is for this country? It is a one-way plane ticket
for more and more New Zealanders to fly to Australia. Why are they going to Australia,
Mr Bennett? They are going to Australia be cause your Government has not created job
opportunities here—

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I move, That the question be now
put.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Who remembers that
fateful night when the sword finally fell on Don Brash, and John Key moved as swiftly
as possible to see Bill English off at the pass? He came out and he announced that he
was ambitious for New Zealand. He was ambitious for New Zealand. Well, where has
all the ambition gone? Where has that ambition gone? Because this Government has lost
its focus, its ambition, on getting people into  jobs and making sure people are paid well
for those jobs. There is no job strategy. Ther e is no strategy for growing jobs. There is
no strategy for growing our economy. The only th ing it can think of to  try to get young
people into work is to cut their wages.
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8639
Well, David Bennett knows. David Bennett knows  that that is old thinking. That is
thinking from the past, because David Bennett said, when he was speaking against this
exact proposal when it was proposed by Roger Douglas: “It is looking at things in a
historical perspective. Well, the world ha s moved on.” Well, in fact, the world has
moved on, but all this National Government can  do—so bereft of ideas that it is—is to
look back into history for failed examples of ways to try to get people into work. It
failed before and it will fail again. David Bennett knew that . He still knows it, and yet
for some reason he will be voting for this bill to carry on today. Under National’s watch
72,000 young Kiwis aged between 18 and 30 have  headed to Australia looking for
better job opportunities.  What else are they looking for? Better wages, of course,
because in Australia they do pay a decent wa ge. They will get a decent wage, and there
is actually a strategy in New Zealand to ge t more people into higher-skilled, better-
paying jobs.
This Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill is a bill that simply
reflects National’s absolute loss of am bition. It has no plan to get young people
working. It has no plan to get young people in to apprenticeships. It  has no plan to get
people higher skills. It has no plan to develop a high-skill, high-wage economy. What
does it have instead? This meagre, pathetic bill, which absolutely lacks any sort of
ambition. But do not ask me. Do not ask me ; ask David Bennett. Ask David Bennett,
who said: “We are denying them their success by holding them at a lower rate than their
ability shows as individuals. ”, and that, actua lly, is why Labour fundamentally opposes
this bill. It allows a form of discrimination th at, absolutely, is not justified. It says to a
young person that because of their age and th eir age alone, they can be discriminated
against. [Interruption] Mr Sabin?

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: I said that member would just hate to see any growth in job numbers.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Ah! Mike Sabin says that we would hate to see any
growth in job numbers. Mr Sabin, where ar e the jobs? Where are the jobs, Mr Sabin?
There are no jobs. That is exactly what this Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage)
Amendment Bill reflects. If there were jobs for people to go to, there would be no
necessity for this bill at all.  If there were jobs, then ther e would be proper competition
in the market for wages and people would be  working. This will not create new jobs.
This will simply shift older people out of the workforce, because employers will be able
to take a job that they offer to someone who actually qualifies for the full adult rate and
give that job to a young pers on who does not qualify for th e full adult rate. It does not
create new jobs. The only way a young person will get a job as a result of this bill is if
somebody else is pushed out of the labour market, Mr Sabin.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Rubbish.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: That is the only way.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Nonsense.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: Mr Sabin can sit ther e and say “Rubbish.” and
“Nonsense.” as much as he likes, but he know s it is not true. He has not actually come
up with a single argument in favour of this bill.

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: There’s plenty of employers who want to give a young person a chance
out there, clearly.

items.speaker: IAIN LEES-GALLOWAY
items.text: If plenty of employers wa nt to give a young person a
chance, why not pay them for the work that they will do? Why not  pay them the rate
that they deserve, Mr Sabin? We are not talking about a charity here. We are talking
about paid employment—the dignity of proper paid employment where a young person
can go to work and know that they will be treated in the same way as anybody else in
that job. That is the dignity that we ar e talking about, not about saying to young people
that they are second-class citizens and do not deserve to get the rate of pay that anybody
8640 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
else in that workplace would be getting. This bill reflects a soft lack of ambition from
the National Party that wants to trap young people in low-skill and low-wage jobs.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): We have had great theatrical speeches
from the other side on the Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill, but I
think I want to draw some of this to a conc lusion, at least in my own thinking. What we
are hearing here is fundamentalism, fundame ntalism at its best. It is fundamentalism
that takes one point and overemphasises it at  the point and agains t everything else. So
let us give this a little bit of context, and let us give this a little bit of consistency, shall
we?
The first is context. We have heard a lot of  things about what this Government is not
doing and so forth and, somehow, that this  young person’s wage is a terrible affront,
because nothing else is happening. There is an  enormous amount that this Government
is doing around jobs, supporting the economy, a nd so forth. Of course, we are talking
about 16 to 19-year-olds, and a lot of them are in educa tion. We can just look at the
continuing results that are coming out of th e education sector. I have been visiting
schools recently and those young people studyi ng there. Of course, we have been
rebalancing things around student loans and allowances. We are increasing funding into
people doing engineering and science. This is a Government committed on a broad
front.
The Opposition will sit here and wax bor ing, if I might say—not lyrical, wax
boring—on a whole lot of elements here that it th inks “Oh, it is terrib le.” It sits in a
context. The Opposition says that the Govern ment is not doing anything for jobs. Well,
let us talk about The Hobbit , let us talk about Skycity, let us talk about Callaghan
Innovation, and let us talk a bout mining. Let us remind ours elves that the Opposition
there said no to all of that. Context is in credibly important. The Opposition is a policy
platform of “no” sayers. It is a naysayer to all of those activities—the mining, Skycity,
Callaghan Innovation, the funding for education and science—and it says no to this
opportunity for young people for a minimum wage.
I want to turn, as well, to the question of  consistency, because, actually, there has
been a great lack of consistency from the Opposition. They are yelling out: “Oh my
Lord, this is a matter of principle.” We hear d it from the Greens. We have heard it from
Labour. It is a matter of principle. But, of  course, the Labour Party does have its own
youth wage as well. Employers said it was unw orkable. It did not work very well, the
same rate as the youth minimum wage. We ha ve heard it from the Opposition “Oh, that
is fine, that is fine. This is different.” It is not actually principled. So to those listening
in and those in the Chamber, to the Oppos ition as it attempted a principled response—
but it is not principled itself—one only needs to look at effectively the youth wage that
the Opposition held.
Also, we have been talking about the living wage, that somewhat arbitrary figure.
Then you look at Supplementary Order Pa per 193 here where $15 is being touted,
which, of course, is no t the living wage. So we have got two levels of  arbitrariness
there. Then, if you really want to push the inconsistency, $15 is actually 80 percent of
the living wage. So, once agai n, the Labour Party is getting all its  numbers muddled
up—all very inconsistent. It is a bit like a bank account that you might have overseas
and you forget it is actually there. Why be consistent? Why be consistent?
For me, really, I come back to where I started—great theatricalness and great
fundamentalism: “We just want to talk about the minimum wage and ignore all the good
things that this Government is doing.” Cont ext is incredibly im portant. And the final
aspect here is that employe rs are not ogres, OK? How many people in the Opposition
have actually run businesses? Businesses want  to employ people. They are encouraging
to employ people. They are not out there to screw every young person down on wages.
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8641
These are Kiwis just like all of us. They are Kiwis like ourselves, wanting to give young
people opportunities. If this House is serious about looking after young people,
providing opportunities—that digni ty of work, Ms Fenton, which Rerum Novarum
spoke about; the dignity of work—we will do all within our powers to help young
people into work.
I want to pick up finally on Mr Sabin’s point, as someone who holds an electorate as
well. It has been interesting that those w ho do not have been pontificating to us. When
the young people come into our offices or we are talking in the schools they want
opportunities. If this is going to  help them, then why not 6 months at 80 percent? But I
come back, finally: theatricalness from the Oppos ition, a lack of prin ciple, certainly no
desire for context, and no consistency in its thinking. Let us move on.

items.speaker: CAROL BEAUMONT
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise to speak for the first
time in this 50th Parliament. But, of course, the matte r we are debating is not one that is
a great pleasure. It is one that Labour opposes, and I proudly join my colleagues in
opposing this Minimum Wage (Starting-ou t Wage) Amendment Bill, because it is
discriminatory. At its very essence this is discrimination.
I want to note the point that my co lleague Dr Megan Woods made about
unemployment, and youth unemployment in par ticular. There is no doubt that there is a
crisis in New Zealand around youth unemployment. It is part of a wider economic crisis
we have in our country of low incomes, of high unemployment, and of high levels of
underemployment. People want work and they  want a decent standa rd of living. We
have a crisis because we have a Government  without any ideas. So what does it revert
to? It reverts to type, of course: straight-out discrimination. It is wrong for young people
to be paid less for doing the same job. That is precisely what this bill does.
Age is not a proxy for skills or experience. As the others have said, there could well
be 18-year-olds who have more experience than a 24-year-old doing the same job.
Youth and age are not proxies for skills and experience. Why should it be that a young
person working at a supermarket at the busiest time of the week gets paid less? So often
in our supermarkets, and anybody who does any shopping knows this—maybe across
the other side of the Chamber people do not  know about this—if you go in at a busy
time in the evening or weekends you will s ee a lot of young people, an d that is also the
busiest time. Our supermarkets are relying on their labour. Why should they be paid less
at the busiest time? It is actually a double whammy. It is ridiculous.
This is a discriminatory piece of legisla tion. It also has a ni ce little twist about
punishing youth beneficiaries to boot. I just th ink this is an absolute disgrace, and that
the consequences of this are going to be so me very negative effects. There are going to
be displacement effects. The Government’s own research says this. Even if there are
jobs created, it will be at the expense of  someone else. It will be replacing somebody
with somebody who is cheaper, not because  people want to employ young people per
se, but because they will be able to employ somebody cheaper.
What happens to young people when they beco me eligible for the full rate? Well, of
course, they could well be replaced by somebody who is cheaper, so older young people
will be disadvantaged. In fact, in combination with the wonderful “90-day No Rights at
Work Act” you could see people on an endless treadmill of never reaching the full rate.
The effects of this in tandem with other Government policies are really very
troubling. I know, for example, that organi sations like the National Council of Women
are worried about the displacement effect s for part-time women workers. Women
workers who are in the workforce in part-t ime jobs—again, maybe in industries like
retail and hospitality where they can get the part-time hours because they need to
balance their family responsibilities and th eir responsibilities in the paid workforce—
will be replaced, potentially, by cheaper young people. So they are concerned about it
8642 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
from the point of view of women part-time wo rkers. That is a displacement effect as
well.
What about the hardship impact on young people? That is also an effect of this piece
of legislation. Often, now, young people’s incomes are a vital part of family income, so
we are actually reducing family income. Often young people are also working to save to
study—something that we would all appl aud. We want young people in tertiary
education. But, again, we are going to make it harder for them to get the money that
they need, or it will mean that, in fact, they have to rack up even higher student loans
than they currently do—again, another negative impact of this legislation.
But what underlies this—and I want to acknowledge the contribution made earlier by
Phil Goff on this—and what this is really about is the typical National Party approach to
our workplaces and to workers’ rights, which is actually around reinforcing the idea that
cheapness is what is really at effect he re, that workers are actually expendable
commodities, and that we do not want to be  ambitious about lifting incomes in New
Zealand. We do not want to create better-qual ity workplaces. We do not want to have
workplaces where, in fact, workers are trea ted with respect and where their ideas and
innovation are what drives productivity. No, we want to continue to  have an approach
that has been National’s approach now for decades—

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I stand to take a call in Part 2, clauses 6 and 7, of the
Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendmen t Bill. I just wanted to start with a
comment, really, that has bemused me during this debate, which is how come increasing
pay motivates bosses and chief executive offi cers, but cutting it is supposed to motivate
young workers? How come? I would really like  the Minister in the chair, the Hon
Michael Woodhouse, to attempt to answer that if he would, or at least a speaker from
the other side, because I do not get it and nor do the thousands of young workers who
are affected by this bill—who see, day in and day out, huge salaries being paid to chief
executive officers, huge amounts of compensa tion given to various people, like Solid
Energy’s Don Elder with $1.3 million to s it on his couch at home, doing nothing—yet
they are supposed to be feeling grateful because this Government is cutting their pay.
8644 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 19 Mar 2013
They are supposed to be buying into the narr ative that we hear again and again from
this Government that work is somehow a charitable act and that employers are offering
a charity. I found it astonishi ng that Mike Sabin could as sert that employers would
create a job for someone because they could pay them $11 an hour. If there is no work
to be done and there is no job, they are not going to do it out of charity. But what we
hear from the National Government is that workers and young workers should be
grateful. They should be grat eful for the opportunity, even though they are going to be
paid less for doing exact ly the same work and they can be sacked within 90 days with
no reason given.
Why should young people be grateful?

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: The good old socialist mantra—that all employers are evil.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: No, it is not, actually. It is about treating young people—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: The good old socialist mantra.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: I am looking forward to Mike Sabin getting on his feet and
answering my first question about why it is OK to pay lots a nd lots of people, and some
people’s chief executive officers, large amounts of money. That is supposed to motivate
them and that is the justification we hear, that young people are supposed to be
motivated by this bill.
I have a couple of things I want to say about  Part 2. In the first part, clause 6, I just
want to check with the Minister in the chair that I am right about this, but the way I read
it is that it amends the Accident Compensa tion Act so that young workers will get 80
percent of 80 percent—is that right? So that  instead of getting 80 percent of the adult
minimum wage, as they do under the current Act, unless they are on the 300 hours or
200 hours, they will get 80 percent of $10.80. I want the Minister to look at that.
Otherwise, I do not see the poin t of that amendment. So what  it seems to be saying is
that people, young workers who go on accident compensation, are going to have their
pay cut even further.
We have already heard today, and we have  already talked about how young workers
are going to be forced off the invalids bene fit and the sickness benefit, otherwise they
will be sanctioned. They will be stood down fr om their benefit for 13 weeks. They will
be punished if they refuse to accept the job that Work and Income deems to be
acceptable. What happens if they get injure d on the job? Rememb er, these are young
workers going into often dangerous situations; it can be very dangerous in some of these
jobs. They are worried about raising issues because they can be sacked in 90 days. They
could have an accident, and then they find themselves on $10.80 an hour. So what this
Part 2 does is reduce the pay for young workers even more if they are injured on the job.
That is so unfair, and I would appreciate th e Minister addressing that and explaining
why the Government thinks that that is fa ir and that young people s hould be forced to
take another pay cut, should they be injured on the job and have to go on accident
compensation.
I want also to address clause 7, which is  the transitional and savings provision in
relation to the minimum new entrant rate. Again, I want to remind the Committee what
the new entrant rate was. It is, in fact, what exists now, but it will go out of existence on
1 May. What that meant was a young worker in their very first job, a 16 or 17-year-old
in their very first job, could be paid 80 percent of the adult minimum wage for 3 months
or 200 hours on a one-off basis. So that was on the basis that they would learn the job
within 3 months or 200 hours, and from then on they would be paid the adult rate.
Of course, what this bill does is remove that. It says that 16 and 17-year-olds have to
learn the job, and it takes them 6 months to learn the job, so they are on $11 an hour,
and then they go to another job and they have  to learn it all over ag ain, so they go back
to $11 an hour. They never get ahead while they  are 16 and 17. That is so unfair. As we
19 Mar 2013 Minimum Wage (Starting-out Wage) Amendment Bill 8645
have heard in this debate, 16 and 17-year-olds are often doing the work, the same job, as
other workers. It is not about  their output or thei r abilities. If it we re, the Government
would not be changing the existing provision s that allow for a training period for a
worker in their very, very first job.
What this bill does is punish 16 and 17-year-o lds. It is not 6 mont hs. It is 6 months,
again, and again, and again. If they happen to lose that job when they are 18 and go on
to a social security benefit,  then if they get a job they  can be punished again. So not
only can they have youth rates all the time, during the period  they are 16 and 17, but it
carries on until they are 18 and 19.
What I do not get about all of this is the lack of unders tanding from the Government
about how discriminatory this is, and how unfair it is that people doing the same job can
be paid less because of their age. We have  not had that kind of discrimination on the
basis of gender, on the basis of race, and on the basis of a whole range of other issues
over the years, for many, many years. That w ould be intolerable. We would not say to
an older worker who is, say, over 65: “Well, you’re not as productive as that worker, so
you’re going to get paid 80 percent.” That would be un acceptable because there are
rules about discriminating ag ainst older people and people on the basis of age. But
somehow, because these are younger pe ople, because they are working and
contributing, they can be picked on by this G overnment. They can be picked off by this
Government.
I go back to what I said at the beginni ng. For some reason, the National Government
thinks these workers are going to be gratef ul for this. Well, I can tell that National
Government that they are not. I have had many contacts. I do not know about Mike
Sabin, about who he talks to in his area. I was interested in Tracey Martin’s contribution
because she lives in the same area, so I was ve ry interested in what she had to say about
it. I talk to a lot of young people. I am in touch with the Same Work Same Pay
movement, which was out the front only a c ouple of months ago, protesting about the
fact that this bill discriminates agains t young people who are tr ying to get ahead and
who are doing the same job.
It is unfair, and it is discriminatory. But worst of all, this is not going to make a damn
bit of difference to youth unemployment. It  is not going to help young people get a job.
If there is no work, there is no job, and employers are not going to perform charitable
acts by giving young people a chance, because they can pay them less. That is so dopey.
That is such a dopey notion. Yet we have heard it again and again.
We all know there is a crisis in youth unemployment, and some of my colleagues
have talked about Labour’s so lutions and Labour’s ideas on that. I cannot fail to come
to the conclusion that this bill demonstrates the absolute dearth of ideas from the
National Party when it comes to deali ng with our young people. Unfortunately, our
young people are going to keep going on the plane to Australia, to better jobs, to a place
where they get treated with respect.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: The almighty Labour Party owns the young people; that’s right.

items.speaker: DARIEN FENTON
items.text: David Bennett should probably just not say too much, given
the speeches he made 3 years ago saying he did not support youth rates. David Bennett
probably should keep quiet.

items.speaker: David Bennett
items.text: Come on; let’s have it again.
